items.title: Add checked-in real-call fraud eval harness, opt-in
items.body:
## Summary
- Prior real-call testing (issues #54/#55/#57) lived only in scratch scripts -- nothing re-verifies those recall numbers against the live models over time, and providers can change model behavior without notice
- Broadens the fraud test corpus (see docs/decisions/0021) to one true-positive/true-negative pair per representative alsoug.com category (cars, real estate, jobs, electronics, services, barter, home/furniture, animals, industrial equipment, general goods), plus fraud archetypes beyond advance-fee/lottery, plus deliberately tricky true negatives that stress precision
- Adds `tests/test_fraud_eval.py`: runs the corpus through the real, live Safety Agent + Policy Agent pipeline end-to-end, asserting aggregate (not per-case) recall/false-positive thresholds, since individual real-call outcomes are inherently probabilistic
- New `fraud_eval` pytest marker, skipped by default (including CI) -- opt-in via `AMM_RUN_FRAUD_EVAL=1`, since a 25-case corpus costs ~35-45 real API calls
- First real run: 10/11 recall (91%), 2/14 false positives (14%)

## Test plan
- [x] `pytest -v` (no opt-in): 95 passed, 1 skipped (fraud_eval correctly skipped)
- [x] `AMM_RUN_FRAUD_EVAL=1 pytest tests/test_fraud_eval.py -v -s` against the real live API: passed, 91% recall / 14% FP rate
- [x] `pre-commit run --all-files`: clean
- [x] AGENTS.md §5 and SPEC.md-adjacent docs/decisions/README.md updated

Fixes #60

items.title: perf(ft8,ft4): WSJT-X-faithful fine-sync tweak + fix FT4 subtract-refine regression (#182)
items.body:
## Summary

- Ports WSJT-X's real Stage-B/C fine-sync algorithm into `fine_refine_3stage` (`ft8/refine_fine.rs`): tweaks a 32-sample Costas reference waveform per trial instead of shifting the whole 3200-sample `cd0` buffer, matching `sync8d.f90`/`ft8b.f90:133-140` exactly. Costas reference table (and `core::sync.rs`'s per-block equivalent, shared across all protocols) now cached for the process lifetime instead of rebuilt per candidate/block.
- Root-causes and fixes a ~10x FT4 decode-speed regression (48.8ms → ~530ms) introduced by an earlier, unrelated LPF-subtract migration (#178-180): `core::dsp::subtract::refine_freq`'s ~50-100-point carrier grid search was fully re-synthesizing the GFSK waveform on every evaluation instead of applying the carrier via a cheap NCO tweak to a once-built carrier-free reference.
- Updates `docs/notes/BENCHMARKS.md`, `FT4_BENCHMARK.md`, `FT8_BENCHMARK.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `README.md` with re-verified recall/speed numbers across every protocol (JT9 5/5→7/7, FT8 JTDX 17/18→18/18, FT4 speed regression documented and fixed).

## Measured results

- `qso3_busy.wav` single-threaded blind decode: ~753ms → ~700ms (~39% faster than real `jt9 -8 -d3`'s own ~1.1s).
- FT4 `decode_frame_subtract`: multi-threaded ~576ms → ~280ms, single-threaded ~894ms → ~602ms.
- Recall unaffected: FT4 6/6 golden, FT8 18/18 JTDX, 6/6 JTDX AP-on extras, 7/8 WSJT-X golden.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test --release --workspace --features full` — all green
- [x] New differential tests (`ls_amp_mag_tweaked_matches_full_resynthesis`, `refine_freq_finds_true_offgrid_carrier`, `tweak_matches_data_shift_reference_within_tolerance`) pass with measured tolerances
- [x] `ft4_wsjtx_sample_recall_vs_golden` 6/6, `ft8_qso3_jtdx_recall` 18/18, `ft8_qso3_apon_recall` 6/6 JTDX extras
- [x] `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features full --no-deps -- -D warnings -D clippy::perf`
- [x] no_std/fixed-point feature-matrix builds (`alloc ft8`, `alloc ft8 fft-extern`, `alloc ft8 fft-extern fixed-point`, etc.)

items.title: chore(npm): drop hardcoded rule count and stale benchmark from the package description
items.body:
The published npm description reads:

> "Open detection standard -- like Sigma, but for AI agents. **751 rules** for prompt injection, tool poisoning, context exfiltration, and MCP attacks. Shipped in Cisco AI Defense. **97.2% recall on NVIDIA garak**."

Both numbers are wrong on the registry right now. The corpus is at 780 on `main` (770 effective), and garak was re-measured to 91.5% on 2026-07-28.

Neither can be kept correct by updating it. The rule count moves most days via auto-crystallize and ecosystem PRs, while the registry description only refreshes on publish — so any number written here is stale between releases by construction. The benchmark has the same problem plus a worse failure mode: a recall figure that drifts upward in a reader's memory while the measured value goes down.

This removes both rather than refreshing them. `data/stats.json` and the README badges stay the place where a current number lives, and they move with the corpus.

Note: the registry listing only changes on the next publish, so this PR fixes the source, not the live description.

items.title: portfolio: show shipped vs in-progress work with real tech specs
items.body:
## Why

The site advertised two projects. Since that copy was written, `services/mtg-api`
went live (2026-08-04) and `mtg-tools` has been live on Cloudflare Pages since
2026-07-31 — neither appeared anywhere, despite the MTG stack dominating recent
commits. The site also had no way to say *how far along* anything is, so
everything read as equally finished.

## What changed

**Model.** `Project` gains `status`, `statusNote`, `spec[]`, and `onResume`.
`stack[]` stays as-is so the résumé's condensed listing is untouched.

**Work section.** Status badge in the card heading, and a labeled tech-spec block
replacing the flat chip row. Live links are suppressed unless `status === "live"`.

**Two new projects.**
- **MTG Card Database** — `in-progress`, "API live · web app in progress".
  Deliberately **described, not linked**: it's live only on a raw `execute-api`
  host with no custom domain.
- **MTG Collection Tooling** — `live`, linked to `mtg-tools.pages.dev`.

**Two factual corrections to existing copy.** Choices' AI suggestions are
subscriber-only (`AI_FREE_USES` 3 → 0), and the game path runs on Lambda
**Function URLs, not API Gateway**.

**Attribution.** Adds the Scryfall / WotC Fan Content Policy notice required by
anything surfacing card data.

**Skills.** Adds a scoped `Python & data` group (Python · FastAPI · Postgres ·
pgvector · embeddings & vector search). This is a deliberate divergence from the
"all backends are Node; don't claim deep Python" line in the vault's
`AI Engineering Job Search.md` — that rule predated `services/mtg-api`. The vault
note has been updated to record the revised, still-scoped guidance (no ML
training, no MLOps).

## Verification

- `npm run build` clean; `tsc -b --strict` enforces the new required fields.
- Rendered in headless Chrome: badges, spec rows, and **no Live link on the MTG
  Card Database card**; attribution renders; spec grid collapses to one column at
  narrow widths.
- Badge contrast computed for both themes — all ≥ 5.3:1, WCAG AA.
- Asserted against the built bundle: no client-project names, no App Store claim,
  no collection valuations, no similarity recall metrics, no "Claude REPL".

## Notes

- **The `/resume` page prints as 2 pages — and did before this change too.** The
  README claims one page. Not a regression here (baseline measured at 2), so left
  alone; worth a separate trim. The résumé shows 3 of the 4 projects via `onResume`.
- No recall/quality numbers are published for the similarity engine, which
  sidesteps a disagreement between `services/mtg-api/OPS.md:120` (gate not met,
  recall@10 0.23) and the vault (gate met, 0.62 after `c99c5f1`). **That stale
  OPS.md line still gates the webapp deploy and is worth reconciling separately.**
- The companion vault commit (`fc499cb`) is committed locally but **not pushed**.

## Ops tasks

None. Content-only frontend change; deploys automatically via
`.github/workflows/portfolio.yml` on merge to `main`. No env vars, repo
variables, SAM parameters, DNS, or third-party configuration required.

items.title: feat(kb): find semantic duplicates by nearest neighbour, and judge them
items.body:
Closes the semantic-duplicate half of ROADMAP Phase 3 — and corrects yesterday's conclusion about it.

## The finding

[#26](https://github.com/jvanheerikhuize/knowledge-base/pull/26) measured that no lexical score can *decide* whether two entries restate each other, and concluded lexical similarity was the wrong signal. The measurement was sound and its regression test still passes. The conclusion was too broad: what failed was the **global threshold**, not the metric.

A global threshold asks *"is this pair similar in absolute terms"*. Absolute similarity is dominated by how much vocabulary a **topic** happens to share, and that varies far more between topics than duplication does within one — so topical neighbours drown real restatements, exactly as measured. Asking instead *"of everything here, which entries is this one **most** like"* cancels the per-entry baseline out.

Re-measured against **seven** hand-written paraphrases planted in the store (28 entries, 378 pairs, no copied phrasing):

| framing | worst positive | pairs to read |
|---|---|---|
| global ranking (the old question) | **#81 of 378** | — |
| per-entry top-1, unioned both ways | **all 7 caught** | **19** (5% of the space) |
| per-entry top-3, unioned both ways | all 7 caught | 55 |

The union is load-bearing, not a detail: a long entry's nearest neighbour is often *not* the short entry restating it, while the reverse holds reliably. Taking a pair when *either* side nominates it took 6 of 7 to 7 of 7 at no extra cost.

## What shipped

**`kb.py candidates [-n 3] [--all]`** — a *blocker*, the cheap recall-oriented half of the standard record-linkage pair. It narrows the pair space and then refuses to rule: roughly one candidate in three to eight is real and no score says which. Token-set Jaccard, not shingles — shingles measure shared *phrasing*, which is what a restatement does not share.

**`kb.py judge A B duplicate|overlap|distinct [--note]`** — the decision, made by an agent reading both entries. Same division of labour `kb.py new` already uses, which keeps `twin-sovereignty-constraint` intact: no embedding model, no vendor call, nothing to keep running.

Verdicts land in `.kb/verdicts.json` bound to a digest of both entries' **description and body, and nothing else**. Re-verifying or relinking does not expire a verdict (neither changes what an entry *claims*); rewriting a body does, and the pair returns marked `TEXT CHANGED SINCE`. That is what makes the sweep incremental — the first pass cost 42 judgements, a new entry costs about `n` more, never another full sweep. A pair standing at `duplicate` deliberately stays in the queue until someone merges it.

**MCP:** `duplicate_candidates` (read) and `judge` (staged write, never commits, dropped entirely under `--read-only`).

Default is `-n 3` rather than the measured-sufficient `-n 1`: recall was already 7/7 at one neighbour, but two positives cleared their nearest rival by under 0.02, and seven positives is too small a sample to spend that margin on.

## First full pass, run in this PR

42 pairs judged: **zero duplicates**, 24 overlap, 18 distinct. Then the incremental design proved itself — adding the write-up entry cost 6 more judgements, not another 42, and editing that entry afterwards correctly reopened exactly its three verdicts.

One real find: `kb-agent-entrypoint-is-agent-md` and `workspace-repo-inventory-drift` describe the same stale `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and were not linked. Now they are. Closest near-miss, recorded for a future `consolidate`: `persist-insight-to-knowledge-base` steps 3–5 restate most of `distill-session-into-memory`.

## Knowledge and docs

- New entry `kb-duplicate-candidates-by-nearest-neighbour`.
- `kb-duplicate-detection-limits` **corrected in place** — measurement and regression test still valid and passing, conclusion now points at the new entry.
- ROADMAP Phase 3 updated, plus the transferable lesson: a negative result can be real, reproducible, correctly tested, and still wrong, when what was measured is one *framing* of the question rather than the question.
- The blocking/matching terminology is cited to Papadakis et al. (ACM CSUR 53(2), 2020) and flagged **read at summary level only** — both PDF mirrors returned 403 from this session. The numbers above are this store's own measurement and rest on nothing in it.
- The measurement harness itself was **not** kept, deliberately, and the entry says so plus what that costs — a research script nothing runs would rot, but re-running the recall numbers means writing fresh paraphrases first.
- README, `memory/AGENT.md`, `AUTONOMY.md` backlog, `DEBRIEF.md`.

## Tests

23 new (`TestCandidates`, `TestCandidatesOverMcp`, `TestJudgeIsAWriteTool`) — **231 total, green**. `kb.py lint` and `triage` clean.

The load-bearing test is the exact inverse of the one from #26: the pair `dupes` must stay quiet about is the pair `candidates` must surface. Both assertions live in the suite, so neither command can drift into the other's job.

Authorised by `AUTONOMY.md` (large chunk → branch + PR + self-merge).

items.title: README: describe TQ+ alongside the existing How-it-works steps
items.body:
## Summary

PR #71 added TQ+ per-coordinate calibration but left the README unchanged. Three updates so the README accurately describes what the codec does without diluting the existing positive framing.

## Changes

**1. Top blurb (line 16).** The "zero data passes" sub-claim is no longer strictly true under TQ+ (one quantile pass during the first add). Reworded to attribute data-obliviousness specifically to the core TurboQuant algorithm — which IS still data-oblivious — and drop the sub-claim:

> Before: "a data-oblivious quantizer that matches the Shannon lower bound on distortion **with zero training and zero data passes**."
> After:  "a data-oblivious quantizer that matches the Shannon lower bound on distortion, **with no codebook training and no separate train phase**."

**2. Feature bullet (line 18).** Same user-facing guarantee, more accurate wording. The codebook is still untrained; TQ+ is internal calibration the user never sees.

> Before: "**No codebook training.** Add vectors, they're indexed. No data-dependent calibration, no rebuilds as the corpus grows."
> After:  "**Online ingest.** Add vectors, they're indexed — no train step, no parameter tuning, no rebuilds as the corpus grows."

**3. New "How it works" step #3 (between rotation and Lloyd-Max).** Quantifies what TQ+ does and the recall it buys, frames as a finite-dim correction to the asymptotic Beta marginal assumption of step 2. Existing steps 3-5 renumber to 4-6.

## What does NOT change

- Online ingest workflow (add vectors, search, no rebuild — same as before)
- "No codebook training" claim (codebook is still deterministic from `(dim, bit_width)`)
- "No rebuilds as the corpus grows" (TQ+ is frozen after the first add, reused by subsequent adds)
- Performance / recall numbers (already updated in #71)

## Test plan

- [x] `git diff main` is README-only, +7/-5 lines
- [ ] Render check on GitHub once pushed

items.title: feat(filter): recall-first defaults (threshold 0.18, boost-only salience, drop contrast)
items.body:
## Recall-first filtering defaults

Calibrated the production filter against real data: **1,530 arachnid images**
(iNaturalist 2021 val) for recall and **10,000 real web images** (Open Images
V7) for the false-positive rate.

### What changed
| Setting | Before | After | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IMGEDGE_THRESHOLD` | `0.5` | `0.18` | The ensemble score caps well below 0.5, so 0.5 blocked almost nothing (~0% recall). |
| Salience weighting | scales up **and** down | **boost-only** | Amplifies large/photographic images; never drags small/stylised ones below threshold. Multiplier clamped to >= 1.0. |
| `IMGEDGE_TIMM_CONTRAST_WEIGHT` | `1.0` | `0.0` | On real web imagery the look-alike contrast cut recall for ~no FPR benefit (it mostly guarded organism look-alikes, rare on the web). Tunable back up. |
| Block terms | bare `spider` | explicit classes + `spider web` | `spider` also matched the non-arachnid *spider monkey*. |

### Result
~**0% -> ~77% recall at ~1% false positives** on the combined real-data set
(vs ~66% for the prior contrast-on baseline at the same FPR).

### Also
- Popup defaults + threshold slider (step `0.01`, default `0.18`) updated to match.
- README env table, `server` docstring, and CHANGELOG updated.
- The two salience unit tests rewritten for the boost-only semantics.

### Validation
- `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check` clean; `pytest -m "not perf"` green.
- Recall/FPR numbers come from offline analysis of `eval` JSON reports (scores
  only -- no images are ever displayed). A fresh end-to-end eval with the
  shipped config will confirm.

items.title: feat(parser): complete the global structural vocabulary (Elixir, Zig, Bash)
items.body:
Refs #224

## The three fixes (global tables only, no per-language code, no `match` on `Language`)

**Elixir** — `import Enum` parses as a `call` node with field `target` (not `function`/`method`/`name`); the argument list is a positional `arguments`-KIND child, never a field. Fixed by:
- `call_callee_field`'s new `target` branch (`structural.rs`), gated on `has_child_of_kind(node, "arguments")` — NOT a field check, since Elixir's `call` node has no `arguments` field at all. Verified via `node-types.json` this doesn't misfire on Swift's own `target`-field nodes (`assignment`/`navigation_expression`/`postfix_expression`/`prefix_expression`/`check_expression`) — none of those five ever carry an `arguments`-kind child.
- `IMPORT_CALL_NAMES` gains `"import"`/`"alias"`/`"use"` (`"require"` was already present).
- `import_call_path` generalized to fall back to a kind-based child scan (no `arguments` field) and to the first LEAF-shaped named node (no `"string"`-kind leaf — Elixir's `alias` node for `import Enum` is a bare, non-string leaf).

This same mechanism also correctly reaches Elixir's ordinary calls (`helper()`) as `CallSite`s — previously wholly unreached. `def`/`defmodule` are ALSO ordinary calls in Elixir's homoiconic macro system (`target`="def", positional `arguments`=[nested call]) and are now correctly classified as calls, not (spuriously) as definitions — Elixir functions remain genuinely unreached as *definitions*, a different, harder problem (macro expansion) than a field-name gap.

**Zig** — `@import("std")` is a `builtin_function` node with ZERO fields at all. Fixed by a new structural fallback, `is_fieldless_call_with_positional_arguments` (`structural_fallback.rs`): a node with NO field-tagged children (checked via a `TreeCursor`'s own `field_name()`, never a fixed field-name table) that carries a positional child of kind `"arguments"` is call-shaped by construction — reuses the SAME "first named child in document order" callee mechanism the existing Swift/kotlin-ng positional-call tier already uses, gated structurally instead of by kind-name vocabulary. Verified via `node-types.json` across every dependency-tree grammar that none of the ten hand-written languages match this gate. `IMPORT_CALL_NAMES` gains `"@import"`.

**Bash** — `source ./foo.sh` is a `command` node whose argument field is singular `argument`, not `arguments` — one character off `call_callee_field`'s exact match (the same gap #226 documented for ordinary calls). Fixed by widening every `arguments`-field check in `call_callee_field` to `ARGUMENTS_FIELD_CANDIDATES = ["arguments", "argument"]`. Verified via a full `node-types.json` survey across every grammar this crate depends on that no OTHER node's unrelated `argument`-named field (C's `unary_expression`, Python's `not_operator`, OCaml's `application_expression`, etc.) gets swept in — each only matches when it ALSO satisfies one of `call_callee_field`'s other required fields, never on `argument` alone. This closes Bash's `command`/call gap generally (`source`, plain commands like `helper`), not just `source`; `IMPORT_CALL_NAMES` gains `"source"`.

None of the three resisted a global fix.

## The three recall numbers, side by side

| sample | size | defs+calls recall | imports recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| original 10 hand-written + Ruby | 11 | 11/11 (100%, unchanged) | 11/11 (100%, unchanged) |
| **12-grammar sample (now TUNED-AGAINST)** | 12 | 9/12 (75%, up from 8/12=67%) | **12/12 (100%, up from 9/12=75%)** |
| **fresh held-out, prevalence-ranked** | 10 (5 applicable) | **2/5 (40%)** among languages where a def+call construct exists at all | **2/5 (40%)** among languages with an import construct |

**The 12-grammar sample is now tuned-against and no longer predicts generalization.** It named Elixir, Bash, and Zig individually as unresolved failures — the exact task this PR closes — so re-measuring against it afterward is not held-out evidence, even though every fix is still a small global table, never per-language code. `structural_wide_sample_tests.rs`'s module doc now says this explicitly.

**The fresh held-out sample is the honest predictor**, selected by GitHub-Linguist real-world prevalence (owner correction mid-task, replacing an initial by-availability list): SQL, HTML, CSS, PowerShell, R, Perl, Groovy, YAML, Dockerfile, HCL/Terraform — none consulted while finalizing the Elixir/Zig/Bash rules above. VB.NET has no published tree-sitter grammar crate (searched under two names, absent) — reported unobtainable, not silently dropped.

**40% is worse than 75%, stated plainly.** Three of the ten languages have NO function/call/import construct in their own grammar at all (HTML, YAML, Dockerfile — pure markup/data/instruction languages) and two more (CSS, HCL) have calls but no function-*definition* construct — all five are excluded from the recall denominator rather than scored as pass or fail, per the metric-applicability discipline the task required. Among the five languages where the metric genuinely applies (SQL, PowerShell, R, Perl, Groovy), only R and Groovy fully recall; SQL and PowerShell miss both columns entirely (verified: SQL's `CREATE FUNCTION` nests its name three fields deep with no `body` field at all; PowerShell's `function_statement`/`command` nodes are entirely fieldless with a kind ending in `"statement"`, outside every vocabulary this engine has). One quality caveat inside an otherwise-recalled language: R's function definitions ARE found, but every one is misnamed `"function"` (the literal keyword text) instead of the real name, due to a grammar quirk that binds the `name` field to the `function` keyword token itself, not to the assignment's LHS where the real name lives.

## What remains unreachable (verified, documented in the diff, deliberately NOT patched to avoid curve-fitting this held-out sample)
- CSS's `@import url(...)`: anonymous keyword kind is literally `"@import"` (with the `@`), outside `IMPORT_KEYWORD_TOKENS`'s current vocabulary; its nested `url(...)` call is reached as a `CallSite` (via the same fieldless-call tier added for Zig) but `"url"` isn't in `IMPORT_CALL_NAMES`.
- HCL's `file("path")` call: its argument-list node is named `"function_arguments"`, not `"arguments"` — outside the fieldless-call tier's exact-kind gate.
- SQL and PowerShell: both fully applicable, both miss entirely — see the held-out test file's trailing comment for the exact field-shape reasons (verified via direct introspection, not guessed).
- Haskell (`bind{name, match{expression}}`) and OCaml (`pattern` field, a third name-field spelling) remain unreached as *definitions* for reasons unrelated to this PR, pre-existing from #226/#230.

## Ratchet held
- `src/parser/mod.rs` diff: empty (`git diff origin/main -- src/parser/mod.rs` — confirmed).
- Bench, measured before AND after via `bench_end_result --all`: `end_result_score` 0.905567805565499, `rust-self` 0.9300070747049568, `typescript-small` 0.8811285364260413 — bit-for-bit identical, as expected since `structural.rs` stays `#[cfg(test)]`-registered only.
- All 5 mandated gates green: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --lib` (441 passed), `cargo test --test graph_accuracy` (41 passed), `cargo test --manifest-path benches/harness/Cargo.toml` (24 passed).
- `cargo test --workspace`: 1389 passed, 0 failed — README's "1200+" claim stays accurate (no bucket crossed).
- File-size cap: every `structural*.rs` file kept ≤500 lines by splitting `structural_fallback_tests.rs` (from `structural_fallback.rs`), `structural_imports_calls.rs` (from `structural_imports.rs`), and moving definition/call emission into `structural_scope.rs`'s new `emit_defs`/`emit_calls`.
- Bootstrap manifest SHA256 in `bin/ensure-binary.sh` updated proactively for the 10 new dev-dependency grammars (same drift PR #226 hit).

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

items.title: feat(score): add open-issue backlog recall with addressed-issue diagn…
items.body:
## Summary
Closes #135
`objective_score` had no signal for whether a plan anticipated the **open-issue backlog**
visible at freeze time T — concrete, knowable-at-T ground truth that maintainers often steer
work from. Adds `backlog_recall` (`benchmark/score.py`): detects which frozen `open_issues`
were addressed in the revealed window (title ↔ commit-subject token overlap) and scores
whether the plan's themes cover those addressed issues (#44). `benchmark/runner.py` now
passes the frozen context's `open_issues` into `objective_score` on replay.

On top of that, adds `addressed_backlog_diagnostics` — for each addressed issue, the issue
number, title, and the specific commit subject that caused it to count as addressed — so
maintainer-facing benchmark output is inspectable instead of just exposing issue numbers
(#135). Diagnostics are purely additive: `backlog_recall`, `addressed_issue_numbers`, and
`matched_issue_numbers` are unchanged whether or not diagnostics are read, and
`objective_component`/`composite_score` don't consume backlog recall at all yet, so no
scoring semantics change.

Git-only runs and an empty backlog degrade gracefully: `backlog_recall` is `0.0` with no
addressed issues and no diagnostics, and every other objective field (module/kind/release/
bump) is provably unaffected by backlog presence or absence.

**Note**: PR #46 (open, unmerged) already proposes the #44 half of this (backlog recall
without diagnostics). This PR supersedes it — same approach, plus the diagnostics #135 asks
for. Please close #46 in favor of this one rather than merging both.

## Related issue

Fixes #44. Closes #135.

## Type of change

- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature / capability
- [x] Benchmark / scoring change
- [ ] Docs / tooling
- [ ] Refactor (no behavior change)

## Area

- [ ] `agent/` (the maintainer agent)
- [x] `benchmark/` (evaluation harness)
- [ ] packaging / CI
- [ ] docs

## How was this verified?

```

items.title: AI-engineering reinforcement (RQ2/RQ4), full-document consistency, and repo cleanup
items.body:
## Summary

Strengthens the **AI-engineering** component of the dissertation with real, additive experiments; propagates the results consistently across all seven documents; cleans the repository for handover; and verifies everything (code + LaTeX + adversarial consistency check). **No fabrication** — every frozen number is reproduced to the thousandth; the frozen models/data are untouched.

## AI-engineering reinforcement (additive, `docs/evaluation/*`)

The negative-on-text RQ4 result and the "thin corpus" RQ2 result were the thinnest spots. Four honest experiments close them:

- **A — Uncertainty (`evaluate_triage_uncertainty.py`):** cluster bootstrap over `(ticker, day)` gives 95% CIs. Marginals are wide (±0.05), so 3-decimal points were misleading — but the *paired* comparison shows adding text lowers PR-AUC **robustly** (`context−full` +0.043, P=1.00), not by chance.
- **B — Embedder benchmark (`evaluate_retrieval_embedders.py`):** FinBERT (domain) **0.420** (worse), E5/BGE (modern) tie MiniLM (~0.51). The embedder choice is now validated **by measurement**, closing the "you argued away FinBERT" critique.
- **C — Retrieval at scale (`evaluate_retrieval_fnspid.py`):** on the multi-year FNSPID corpus (~80k headlines) **P@5 = 0.595** (> 0.514 preliminary); direction-consistency 0.708 sits at the 0.688 chance floor, quantifying *theme ≠ direction*.
- **D — RQ4 fair re-test (`evaluate_triage_fairtext.py`):** tuned regularisation + PCA-reduced text + FinBERT — the text recovers to context level (0.499→0.533) but **never beats volatility (0.542)**. The negative result is robust, not an under-fit artefact (honest nuance: the frozen 0.496 was partly dimensionality-depressed).

These are **integrated bilingually** into the thesis (ch2 embedder benchmark; ch6 RQ2 "validated at scale" + RQ4 robustness clause) and propagated to the paper, both slide decks, the study guide, and the defence materials.

## Repository cleanup & consistency

- Removed impression-management / "reads-as-software-spec" framing from all outputs (EN + PT); the honest AI-use declaration stays.
- Removed `docs/_archive/` (6), `product_critique.md`, `ROOT_PROMPT_CLAUDE_CODE.md`, `evaluation_triage_smoke.md`, and the "hide-history" migration doc; added a top-level `INDEX.md`.
- Synced drifting counts (tests, slides, pages) to stable values; thesis page counts corrected to **90 (EN) / 92 (PT)**.

## Defence materials

`docs/defence/guiao_de_defesa.md` (recall pack: numbers, per-RQ verdicts, 15-min structure, formulas explained) and `docs/defence/simulacro_defesa.md` (pressure-chain mock viva), both updated to the reinforced results. `docs/design/usefulness_study.md` gives a runnable RQ3 usefulness-study protocol + turn-key kit.

- **Gates green:** `ruff` clean; `pytest` exit 0 (200+ tests, gated telegram/sbert skipped); all LaTeX compiles with 0 errors and 0 undefined references (thesis 90/92 pp, slides 19/19, paper 4 pp, guide 77).

items.title: feat(apps): add sequential call cascade
items.body:
## Summary

A single call has one target. This app is a search across several: candidates that must
first be ordered, criteria that are only settled during the conversation, a verdict per
call, and a state that carries across calls — who was asked, and what it failed on.

Four kinds of condition stay apart:

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `must` | without it there is no deal |
| `boundary` | up to here and no further |
| `concession` | available, but staged |
| `wish` | improves the ranking, blocks nothing |

**A concession is an authorisation, not a hint.** A result that used a tier nobody granted
is rejected exactly like an offer above the boundary — an agent that bought the deal with
authority it was never given exceeded its mandate, and its yes does not count. A later tier
played before an earlier one is rejected too, because an agent that plays every card at
once gives away more than a person would.

An unknown outcome halts the cascade rather than being read as a refusal, an acceptance or
an unreachable line. The next call would otherwise be built on a guess, and a cascade that
guesses spends the user's remaining candidates on a mistake.

The example is dinner; the pattern is not. A dentist appointment within 30 km, a tradesman
with a free slot, a spare part in stock — same mechanism, different subject.

Full application: <https://github.com/lukisch/hungrycall>

cd apps/python/hungrycall-cascade && python -m pytest -q
........................                                                 [100%]

python scripts/validate_repository.py

```

Both were run on this branch. The validator was also run on the unmodified upstream
checkout first, so a green result here is a comparison and not just an assertion.

## Real-world side effects

None. There is no live transport and no `--live` flag in this edition — it cannot dial even
if configured to. No account, no API key, no network request of any kind. Every response
comes from the fixture file, and the run is labelled `FIXTURE RUN -- SIMULATED, NO CALL
PLACED` on its first line.

## Cancellation

One pass, in order. There is no scheduler and no retry, so nothing runs later or repeats by
itself. Stopping the process stops it before the next candidate; nothing was dispatched, so
nothing needs recalling.

Fictional numbers only, from the `+1 555-0100…555-0199` range reserved for fiction. Numbers
are validated as E.164 before processing and masked in every output path — report,
structured result and error message alike. A regression asserts that no full number appears

items.title: feat(apps): add multi-recipient response aggregator
items.body:
## Summary

Calling twenty people is the easy part. The hard part is the sentence afterwards:
*"eleven of them prefer Tuesday."* Eleven of how many? Of those who answered, or of those
who were invited? And if four never picked up, do they count as indifferent?

They do not. This app keeps five groups apart — `answered`, `refused`, `unreached`,
`pending`, `unknown` — and names the denominator in the report itself: `4 answered / 6
invited`, with a generated caveat listing exactly who is missing and stating that they are
not counted as indifferent.

Three rules follow, and they are what the regressions defend:

- **Silence about one option is unknown, not a no.** The shipped schedule fixture makes
  this case on purpose: for Wednesday, `cannot` is empty — nobody objected — and the slot
  still does not count as agreed, because one respondent never mentioned it. A naive tally
  would call that a match.
- **A tie stays a tie.** The opinion fixture ends 2–2 and stays there. Nothing breaks the
  draw, because the caller was not asked to decide anything.
- **Conditions, abstentions and reasons survive the merge**, and every coded reading keeps
  the raw sentence beside it, so a reader can check the interpretation instead of trusting
  it.

A catch-up round calls only the `pending` and the `unreached`. Someone who answered is
done, and someone who refused has given their answer — calling them again is not a
catch-up.

items.title: feat: recursive (RLM) hunk-walk by default, with opt-out and an A/B benchmark
items.body:
## What this does

Started as a small cleanup (drop an orphaned RLM eval spike) and grew into making **RLM-style recursive review a real, default-on feature** — backed by a benchmark.

When a single file's diff exceeds the per-call token budget (`max_input_tokens`), the engine now **walks it hunk-by-hunk** — each hunk reviewed in its own focused call, findings merged — instead of sending the whole file in one call and letting the tail fall out of the model's attention. Files within budget are still reviewed whole (context preserved). Inline-comment positions stay bound to the real diff.

## Changes

- **Engine**: `compress.split_patch_into_hunks` + `batch_files(recursive=...)`; the engine decomposes over-budget files into per-hunk mini-diffs (each carrying its file header) and batches them normally.
- **Config / surfaces**: `ReviewConfig.recursive` (**default on**), exposed as `--recursive/--no-recursive` (CLI), the `recursive` Action input, and a `config set` key. The local CLI (`lgtmaybe review`) walks recursively too.
- **Benchmark**: `evals/rlm.py` is a repeatable A/B benchmark runnable via CLI against a local model — runs both strategies `--repeats` times over the RLM fixtures and reports recall mean/min/max/spread + token cost + a verdict. A second fixture (`rlm-pipeline`) was added so results don't rest on one diff. The `rlm-bench` workflow runs the same command per matrix leg.
- **Docs**: simplified model guidance — **use a coding model**, and **bigger/newer is more accurate** (our numbers are for the small `qwen3.5:4b` we tested). README, `run-locally-with-ollama`, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, and the generated config reference updated.
- **CI / misc**: bumped the `e2e-ollama` smoke model to `qwen3.5:4b`; removed the orphaned spike.

## Benchmark result (qwen3.5:4b, 8 runs/strategy, two fixtures pooled)

| strategy | mean recall | range | spread | tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| whole (original) | 61% | 45–82% | 36 pts | ~17.0k |
| **recursive (RLM)** | **88%** | 82–100% | 18 pts | ~40.4k |

Recursive averaged **+27 points** of recall and its *worst* run matched the whole-file method's *best* — a real effect, not run-to-run noise — while being more stable, at **~2.4× the tokens**. These fixtures fit the context window, so this is the *focus* / "lost-in-the-middle" effect, **not** truncation avoidance. Measured on a **small** model, where the focus effect is largest — a bigger, newer coding model catches more across the board and leans on this less. `--no-recursive` is there for anyone who wants the cheaper whole-file pass.

## Testing

TDD throughout (compress, engine, models, config, eval plumbing). Full gate green (lint / format / mypy / pytest). The recall numbers come from the live `rlm-bench` sweep, not the pytest gate (model-quality stays out of the deterministic gate by design).

| `docs/ADOPTION.md` | rollout owners | pilot → measure → scale playbook, metrics framework, steady-state loops, honest cost table |
| `docs/EVALS.md` | numbers auditors | moved from `eval/README.md` (git rename; inbound links updated) |

## README rewrite

- Positioning table + harness-loop diagram up front; documentation index at the end.
- New "How it makes agent output predictable" section — five layered mechanisms, naming the nine MUST review principles (SOLID/DRY/KISS/SoC/…) and the clean-architecture dependency rule.
- Fixed the stale What-you-get tree (it listed 5 of 7 agents — `spec-steward` and `acceptance-verifier` were missing) and replaced the comment-crammed skills list with a family table mirroring the generated catalog.
- **Fixes a real inconsistency:** the old "Supported model floor" section cited pre-round-3 numbers (recall 1.000/32, adherence 0.952) that contradicted the committed `eval/baseline.json`. The new "Measured, not believed" section uses the current baselines (0.934/43 routing + gated FP rate, 0.778 adherence with safety 0.615, 6/6 mutation kills, decay 0.33 @ ~90k tokens). Same practical conclusion (Haiku-class needs the deterministic permission layer), now consistent with the repo's own data.

## Notes for review

- **Stacked on #5** (`feat/eval-expansion`): the docs cite the round-3 baselines and history records committed there, so this PR targets that branch and should merge after it (GitHub will retarget to `main` automatically).
- All numbers quoted in the docs trace to `eval/baseline.json` / `eval/history.jsonl` at HEAD — nothing is invented.
- Mermaid diagrams throughout (6 in ARCHITECTURE, 6 in AGENTS-AND-SKILLS, 2 each in WHY/ADOPTION, 1 in README) — worth a render check in the GitHub preview.
- Also commits the latest mutation-run record in `eval/history.jsonl` (6/6 kill rate).

### [`v2.1.224`](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code/releases/tag/v2.1.224)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code/compare/v2.1.223...v2.1.224)

#### What's changed

- Added self-hosted environments: `claude self-hosted-runner` turns your own machines or containers into a place Claude Code web, mobile, and desktop sessions can run, on Team and Enterprise plans
- Added `archive` plugin source: install plugins from a zip over HTTPS without git or npm, with optional SHA-256 pinning
- Added a cancel-and-confirm step when removing an unavailable paste changes a command's text
- Added `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_REGION_PREFIX` env var for Bedrock to prefer a specific cross-region inference profile over the `AWS_REGION`-derived one
- Added `crossSessionInbound` and `dialogExpiry` settings: cross-session messages sent to a session running with bypassed permissions are held for your approval, and messages to other sessions auto-deliver
- Added sandbox credential-masking options: `extract` and `onExtractNoMatch` for structured env values, `decode: "jwt"` with `maskClaims` for JWT-aware masking, and `awsPairs`/`sigv4` for AWS SigV4 re-signing; these need `network.tlsTerminate` and are honored only from user, managed, or `--settings` settings
- Added cross-session `SendMessage`: Claude Code sessions can now message each other, on any of your machines, with `ListAgents` to discover them (macOS and Linux)
- Fixed long (>200 char) project paths resolving to another project's session directory under a shared sanitized prefix; session list, rename, fork, delete and `/resume` no longer cross projects
- Fixed `SendMessage` reporting "Message sent" when the write to a teammate's inbox had actually failed; failed deliveries are now reported as errors
- Fixed sandbox filesystem deny entries written with a trailing slash (e.g. `denyRead: "~/.aws/"`) being silently bypassable on Linux and macOS
- Fixed sandbox violation details never appearing in Bash tool results; Claude now sees which file or network access was denied and why
- Fixed MCP tools that connect mid-turn being deferred for tool search without their names announced to the model
- Fixed plugin install records being silently corrupted when the same plugin is installed in multiple projects
- Fixed recalled or restored paste content occasionally attaching wrong data or silently losing text when the paste had aged out or placeholder numbers collided
- Fixed copy-on-select on Wayland sometimes not reaching the clipboard; the two selection writes no longer race
- Fixed the feedback survey's transcript share silently failing on long sessions; a failed share now shows an error instead of a success message
- Fixed Remote Control auto-start intermittently failing with "Remote credentials fetch failed" on a cold start with a stale login token
- Fixed Remote Control and SDK clients showing a blank "(no content)" message after `/clear` and other output-less commands
- Fixed a Remote Control session recreated after its server session expired uploading prior local conversation history into the new session
- Improved fullscreen mode to keep the full pre-compaction history in scrollback across repeated compactions, instead of only the most recent interval
- Improved Remote Control: attached web and mobile clients now see compaction progress and the post-compaction boundary instead of a silent pause; `/clear` resets now propagate to attached clients
- Improved Remote Control: connection failures now show a persistent failure indicator with details and a reconnect shortcut, instead of only an 8-second toast
- Removed the 200-subagent-per-session spawn cap; long-running sessions no longer refuse new agents (concurrency and depth limits still apply)
- Changed managed settings: the approval prompt no longer re-appears after re-login or org switching when the organization's settings are unchanged
- Changed the feedback-survey transcript share: with your consent it now also uploads the last request's model settings — the system prompt (which includes your `CLAUDE.md` instructions), tool definitions, and model parameters. Secrets are redacted as before, and these fields are dropped first if the share is too large
- Changed the Bash tool description to always note that command output is displayed to the model, not reliably to the user
- Changed recalled paste placeholder numbers to renumber when accepted into the input
- Changed Remote Control to archive the stale server session instead of leaving a dead one listed when a fresh session is minted after compaction or `/resume`
- \[VSCode] Fixed the extension showing Remote Control as connected after the connection failed
- Fixed a session resume silently reconnecting Remote Control after the user turned it off (`--resume`, SDK hosts, and the VS Code extension)
- \[VSCode] Fixed sessions not honoring `remoteControlAtStartup` when explicitly enabled

### [`v2.1.223`](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code/releases/tag/v2.1.223)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code/compare/v2.1.222...v2.1.223)

#### What's changed

- Added a warning when workflow agents, forked skills, slash commands, or resumed background agents' requested subagent model is restricted and the parent model runs instead
- Added a `/teleport` hint in cloud sessions showing how to continue locally with `claude --teleport <session id>`
- Fixed a Bash permission bypass where a crafted command could hide parts of itself from permission checks
- Fixed permission prompts so commands padded with tabs or invisible Unicode can no longer hide part of the command from the approval dialog

- Fixed a permission gap where an agent definition's `bypassPermissions` mode ignored the org bypass-permissions disable policy

#### What's changed

- Fixed renaming a session from Claude Code Desktop or claude.ai not updating the CLI's session name; session names from every rename surface are now sanitized
- Fixed plugin- and org-delivered skills named after terminal-only built-ins (e.g. `/help`, `/feedback`) being un-invocable in non-interactive sessions

- Improved auto mode: permission checks for parallel tool calls are now cache-efficient, and switching modes while a check is pending reliably prompts instead of applying the stale result

- Improved `/ultrareview` error messages when a repo shares no history with its base: a checkout with no branches is now refused up front with advice to create one, and refusal hints no longer suggest `git fetch --unshallow` on clones that are already complete
- Improved Windows startup: process creation times are now read via a native kernel32 call instead of spawning PowerShell, so endpoint security tools that gate `powershell.exe` no longer prompt

It turns a decision you can't answer alone into a Markdown questionnaire for the one person who can — filled in async, or worked through together in a meeting.

  Its defining move is that it grills you about the **send**, not the subject: a normal grilling session interrogates the topic, which is exactly what you can't answer here, so the interview asks only who the questionnaire is going to and what you need back, then aims every question at the gap between the two.

  Now wired as a promoted skill — plugin entry, top-level + Productivity READMEs under **User-invoked**, a docs page at `docs/productivity/to-questionnaire.md`, and a Standalone route in `ask-matt` framing it as the inverse of `/grill-me` (mine someone else, not yourself).

It generates an interactive bash script that walks a human through a manual procedure — third-party setup, a one-off migration, an A→B state transition — opening each URL, saying what to click, capturing the values, and writing them into `.env` files and GitHub Actions secrets.

  The delightful UX is pre-solved by the bundled `template.sh` (progress with time-remaining, confirmation gates, cross-platform URL opening including WSL, hidden secret entry, idempotent `.env` upserts, `gh secret`/`gh variable` writes with graceful degradation, closing skip summary). Everything above the `STAGES` marker is a fixed library that's never hand-edited — the skill's job is only to scope the procedure and author its **stages**.

  Engineering rather than Productivity: it reads `.env*`, `docker-compose*`, framework config and every `secrets.*`/`vars.*` reference in `.github/workflows/` to scope itself, writes CI secrets, and verifies its output with `bash -n` and `shellcheck`.

  Because it is model-invoked, the agent can reach for it the moment it hits a step only a human can perform, instead of dumping numbered instructions into the chat and hoping you follow them. Typing `/wizard` works exactly as before — model-invocation only ever *adds* the agent's reach. The description is written as the pointer that decides when it fires: what it produces, four trigger branches (provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, a one-off migration or cutover), and an explicit non-trigger — don't invoke it for steps the agent can perform itself. Work an agent can do, an agent should do; the wizard is for the clicks, approvals and dashboard trips you would not hand to one. The stage-list confirmation before a line is written now doubles as the proposal when the agent fires it mid-build.

  Now wired as a promoted skill — plugin entry, top-level + Engineering READMEs under **Model-invoked**, a docs page at `docs/engineering/wizard.md`, and a Standalone route in `ask-matt` for the steps only a human can take. Model-invocation also puts it out of the reach of [#​693](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/693), which drops user-invoked skills from the listing on Claude's desktop and web surfaces.

- [#​763](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/763) [`77d207e`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/77d207ef03219cc603e2832e1159cbdd1c91818e) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Reshape the **`prototype`** skill around two ideas: the demo is **a single shareable HTML file**, and the prototype is **a primary source**.

  The logic branch now produces one self-contained file (plain HTML/CSS/JS, no build, no server) instead of a terminal app — a non-developer can open it by double-click and drive it in their own domain language: a labelled state panel, always-available free-play buttons, and a set of tabbed **guided walkthroughs**, each a scenario with the ordered buttons to press underneath it. The portable pure-logic module still lifts into the real code; the HTML shell is the throwaway.

  Throwaway no longer means deleted. Rather than being removed once it has answered its question, the prototype is captured as runnable evidence on a throwaway branch (`prototype/<name>`) out of main, with a context pointer to it left on the implementation issue — so the main branch keeps only the validated decision while the exploration stays findable. The answer (verdict + question) is still captured durably in an issue/ADR/commit.

- [#​536](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/536) [`42a5b70`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/42a5b70fcacc7baff1977b13f3919fb2f63af14e) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Ship the skill set as a native **Claude Code plugin**, listed in Claude Code's official marketplace. You can now subscribe to the promoted skills as a managed, read-only bundle instead of copying editable files:

  ```bash
  claude plugins install mattpocock-skills
  ```

  Or, from inside a session:

  ```
  /plugin install mattpocock-skills
  ```

  There is no marketplace to add first — the official marketplace is configured by default.

  `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` carries the full plugin metadata (version, description, author, license, keywords) and the explicit list of promoted skills. `skills.sh` remains the universal installer (and the path for Codex and other harnesses today); a native Codex plugin is deferred — see `.agents/adr/0002-ship-as-a-claude-code-plugin.md` for why.

- [#​751](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/751) [`355fa74`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/355fa7420b418af838998f7ec4365ceda1c8dfcc) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Add **`wait-what`** — a one-word corrective for model verbosity. Type it the moment a message doesn't land, and the agent re-pitches it: a little context, ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, and the ubiquitous language from your `CONTEXT.md`. User-invoked, three lines long.

  The mechanism is the name. Concision skills fail by growing — a 400-line skill still leaves the model verbose — so this one is a single precise leading word and nothing else. Names that describe the *output* (`/tldr`, `/no-fluff`) make the model clip words and lose you further; naming the *listener's* state asks for both halves at once, fewer words **and** the context you were missing. It also reuses the leading words already in your global `CLAUDE.md`, so the skill, `CLAUDE.md` and every `CONTEXT.md` reach for the same tokens.

  It repairs one message; it doesn't prevent the next one. The cure for jargon is a shared language built upfront with `/grill-with-docs`; this is what you reach for when you don't have one yet.

- [#​763](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/763) [`77d207e`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/77d207ef03219cc603e2832e1159cbdd1c91818e) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Name the `/wayfinder` unit a **decision ticket**, and burn research tickets down with subagents.

  People kept reading a wayfinder ticket as an ordinary *implementation* ticket — a slice of a build to execute — when wayfinder uses them as **decision tickets**: questions whose resolution is a decision. The skill description and its opening line now introduce the term (and say what makes it one), with the `ask-matt` / engineering README blurbs and the docs page matching — while "ticket" stays the everyday word once the term is established. `CONTEXT.md` records **Decision ticket** as a domain term, so the "avoid: ticket" guidance no longer contradicts wayfinder's deliberate use of the word.

  Research tickets are no longer parked for a separately-launched session. Research stays a real ticket type — it's a genuine shared blocker that downstream decisions hang on, and that dependency is exactly what the frontier's blocking edges exist to render. What changes is how it's resolved: because research is AFK, charting doesn't stop and read it. After creating the tickets, the charting session fires a `/research` subagent for each research ticket to burn it down in parallel, capturing the findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer. Research tickets are the one exception to *one ticket per session*.

- [#​763](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/763) [`77d207e`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/77d207ef03219cc603e2832e1159cbdd1c91818e) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - **Breaking:** rename **`writing-great-skills`** → **`writing-for-agents`**, restructure it, and add a new leading word.

  The reference now covers any document an agent consumes — skills, `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`, docs reached by a pointer — not just skills. `GLOSSARY.md` is merged into `SKILL.md` (one authoritative treatment per term; the `_Avoid_` synonym lists and the standalone Predictability definition are gone); the skill-only mechanics (frontmatter, model- vs user-invoked, router skills, the invocation cut of splitting) are disclosed to a new `SKILL-MECHANICS.md`. The skill is now **model-invoked**: it fires when creating or editing skills or modifying `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. `ask-matt`'s pointer updated. Reinstall under the new name; the old name is gone (no alias).

  The pruning section gains **cache**. Single source of truth now reaches past the document into the environment — `package.json` scripts, config files, directory layout, `--help` output are themselves authoritative, so a doc that restates them is a cache of a lookup, earning its load only when the lookup is expensive. The positive target: cache what the agent cannot find by looking (unwritten conventions, the reason behind a choice, gotchas no config confesses), and leave one-file, one-command lookups to the environment, where they cannot go stale.

- [#​533](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/533) [`45afd80`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/45afd8074a8b7de5fe073845d080fa9dd6c429fa) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Add a YAGNI scoping filter to the **`improve-codebase-architecture`** skill's Explore step. Instead of scanning the whole repo evenly, it now scopes to where change is actually landing: if you name a direction it takes it, otherwise it reads the last \~20 commit messages to bias exploration toward actively-developed paths. A deepening opportunity in code nobody touches is a refactor you'll never cash in — the leverage only pays off where you keep editing — so the report stops tidying dormant corners of the repo.

##### Patch Changes

- [#​763](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/763) [`77d207e`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/77d207ef03219cc603e2832e1159cbdd1c91818e) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Sharpen `/ask-matt` — the router now covers phase boundaries, the two wayfinder mistakes, and two skills it never mentioned.

  **Phase boundaries.** A **phase** is a chunk of work inside a session — the grilling, the implementation, the QA — and the boundary between two of them is where you decide what to do with the context you've built. The two-bullet `Crossing sessions` section is replaced by a decision tree carrying all five options in order (**continue**, `/clear`, `/handoff`, **subagent**, `/compact`), with the reasoning disclosed in a new `PHASE-BOUNDARIES.md`. Three fixes come with it:

  - **`/handoff` was oversold.** It read as the general bridge between context windows. It's narrow: you need it only when something has to *travel* — a new harness, a new directory, a colleague, or a side task forked mid-phase. What it buys is portability.
  - **`/compact` is the default, not the first reach.** It sits at the bottom of the tree, after the four cheaper or more precise questions above it. Starting there produces a session that's confidently wrong about whatever the summary flattened.
  - **Two branches were missing entirely.** **Continue** is the one to rule out first — it's the only move that keeps the conversation as a primary source rather than a summary of one — and a **subagent** handles anything scoped tightly enough to run AFK.

  Context hygiene's escape hatch now says `/compact` rather than `/handoff` (same harness, same directory, at a boundary — the handoff clause doesn't apply), and the smart zone figure is updated from \~120k to \~150k tokens.

  **Wayfinder routing.** The two mistakes people most often make with the heaviest, most cognitively demanding flow:

  - **Over-reaching for it.** It's slower and denser than a single grill, so it's flagged as the heaviest flow and reserved for the idea that genuinely won't fit one session — a well-scoped feature belongs on `/grill-with-docs`, not here.
  - **Losing the way at the handoff.** When the map clears, wayfinder hands off, it doesn't build: merge onto the main flow at `/to-spec` (which collapses the map's linked decisions into a buildable plan) rather than looping the map straight into `/implement`. Straight-to-`/implement` is only for efforts that turned out genuinely small.

  **Missing routes.** `/grilling` and `/resolving-merge-conflicts` were absent from the router altogether and are now in it, and `grill-me` splits from `grill-with-docs` on whether you are in a working directory.

- [#​502](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/502) [`44eed54`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/44eed545186ffd0263e8004867750b80cfddd215) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Make `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` friendlier and align the local-markdown tracker with the current spec.

  - **Triage labels** are now asked about only when the `triage` skill is installed, and then as a single recommended-yes question ("keep the default triage labels?") instead of an override interrogation. When `triage` isn't installed, the section — and `docs/agents/triage-labels.md` — are skipped.
  - **External PRs as a request surface** is no longer a setup question. The GitHub/GitLab templates still carry the flag, defaulted off; a user can flip it in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` later.
  - **Domain docs** default to single-context without asking; multi-context is only offered when the repo shows monorepo signals.
  - **Local-markdown tickets** are now one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md` — never a single combined `tickets.md`. `/to-tickets` and the local issue-tracker template now agree, and the spec file is `spec.md` (not `PRD.md`) to match `/to-spec`.

  Docs pages for `setup-matt-pocock-skills` and `to-tickets` re-synced.

- [#​532](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/532) [`170ad48`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/170ad48655825783d0193e850e31a9aac957bb95) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Reword **`grilling`** for general use. Its description and body no longer scope the interview to a software plan: "this plan" → "this", "enact the plan" → "act on it", and "exploring the codebase" → "exploring the environment". The technique is unchanged; it now reads as a stress-test of any plan, decision, or idea.

- [#​593](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/593) [`a4b2009`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/a4b2009a1a3ac9575506c10b4c84f08f9bba7a38) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Rework **`grilling`** from one-question-at-a-time to round-by-round. It now maps the decision tree and asks the whole **frontier** — every question whose prerequisites are already settled — in a single numbered round, then recomputes the frontier from the user's answers and asks the next round. Same 13 questions land in \~3 rounds instead of 13. Facts the environment can answer are dispatched to background sub-agents so research never blocks the round: only questions downstream of a running exploration wait for it. The session ends when the frontier is empty.

  Every question in a round is emitted in one fixed shape — `❓ **Q1** - **<title>**`, then the body (prose or multiple choices), then the recommendation on its own `➡️` line. A round reads as a scannable numbered list with each recommendation visually separated from the question, so you can answer by number instead of quoting questions back.

  `grill-me`, `grill-with-docs` and `triage` run the frontier a round at a time as well — `triage`'s grill step and `grilling`'s Codex `short_description` now say so instead of describing the old rhythm. The opt-out for one-question-at-a-time (a line in your global `CLAUDE.md`) is unchanged.

- [#​752](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/752) [`c66bdee`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/c66bdeeee002d81e3f8b21403c07f9a0d7bea6da) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Remove six skills from the repo. None of them was in the Claude Code plugin, but all six were installable through [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills), which serves every skill in the repo — so this is what leaves that listing, and where each one went.

  Four retired skills, each already absorbed by a skill that does the job better:

  - **`ubiquitous-language`** → **`/domain-modeling`**, which builds and maintains the whole domain model rather than dumping a glossary from one conversation.
  - **`design-an-interface`** → **`/codebase-design`**. Nothing is lost: the "design it twice" technique — parallel sub-agents generating radically different designs, from Ousterhout — ships inside that skill as `DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md`.
  - **`qa`** → **`/triage`** and **`/to-tickets`**.
  - **`request-refactor-plan`** → **`/to-spec`** and **`/improve-codebase-architecture`**.

  And two that were only ever mine — tied to my own machine and never meant for anyone else. The `personal/` bucket goes with them:

  - **`edit-article`**
  - **`obsidian-vault`**, which hardcoded a path to my own Obsidian vault.

  `skills/deprecated/` stays as a bucket, now empty. `skills/in-progress/` is unchanged and is now described for what it actually is: a beta channel, published on purpose, installable one skill at a time through skills.sh.

- [#​734](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/734) [`a2f9333`](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/a2f9333669ff53db762c87ecda5a15442060a3be) Thanks [@​mattpocock](https://redirect.github.com/mattpocock)! - Finish the `to-prd` → `to-spec` rename: "spec" is now the only term in the shipped text.

  - **`to-spec`** no longer opens with "you may know this document as a PRD" — the parenthetical is dropped from the skill and its docs page. The local-markdown tracker template drops the same hedge.
  - **`code-review`** talks about the originating issue/spec rather than issue/PRD, in its frontmatter description, its two-axis summary, and the spec-source search order. Both READMEs re-synced.
  - **The GitHub and GitLab tracker templates** now say "Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub/GitLab issues" — they had been left on "PRDs" when the local template was updated, so the stale term propagated into every repo they were written into.
  - **`docs/engineering/research.md`** pointed at `https://aihero.dev/skills-to-prd`, a dead slug for the renamed skill; it now links `to-spec` like the other nineteen docs pages do.

  The CHANGELOG and existing changesets still name PRDs where they document the rename itself, which is correct.

</details>

items.title: Fill in the benchmark rows and reconcile the onnx feature with reality
items.body:
## Summary

Two long-open honesty gaps, closed.

### 1 — Fill in the public benchmark page (closes #44)

`docs/benchmarks/2026-04-25-mnemo-v0.3.4.md` shipped in **April 2026** with mnemo's own rows `_pending_`, waiting on an authenticated LLM-judged nightly run that never landed (the OpenAI/Anthropic/gated-HF secrets in #44 were never wired). They're **populated now**, from a **real embedder** on this machine — no estimates.

- **Harness:** Rust `semantic_recall_bench` (credential-free retrieval-quality metric that `baseline.json` has recorded since 2026-06-29).
- **Embedder:** Ollama **`nomic-embed-text`, 768-dim**, local, cosine HNSW — never NoopEmbedding.
- **Dataset:** bundled `longmemeval_m` 45-record slice, eval = 23 held-out queries, 5 seeds.
- **Machine:** Apple M4 (10-core), 16 GB · macOS 26.5.2 (arm64) · rustc 1.97.0 · Ollama 0.32.3 · 2026-08-03.
- **Reproduce:** `ollama pull nomic-embed-text && cargo run --release -p mnemo-locomo-bench --bin semantic_recall_bench`

**Retrieval-quality numbers (this run):**

| Strategy | recall@5 | recall@10 | MRR | p50 ms | p95 ms | p99 ms |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `auto` | 0.809 | 0.957 | 0.604 | 42.1 | 50.2 | — |
| `vector_only` | 0.826 | 1.000 | 0.806 | 39.0 | 51.2 | — |
| `hybrid_rrf` | 0.826 | 0.957 | 0.766 | 42.1 | 48.3 | — |
| `graph_boosted` | — | — | — | — | — | — |

**Losses published alongside wins** (a benchmark where the author always wins reads as marketing):
- mnemo's **default `auto` RRF fusion loses to pure `vector_only` on MRR (0.604 vs 0.806)** — the equal-weight RRF drags in BM25 candidates; tuning (`hybrid_rrf`, MRR 0.766) recovers most but still doesn't beat pure vector.
- **BM25 loses on every metric** (recall@5 0.739, MRR 0.586).

**Honest framing:** these are **retrieval** numbers, *not* the LLM-judged QA of the reference leaderboard (Hindsight/Letta) — a different axis. `vector_only` recall@10 = 1.000 means "the gold doc was in the top 10 for all 23 held-out queries on this small slice," not that mnemo out-answers Hindsight. `graph_boosted` and `p99` are left explicitly empty with one-line reasons (no distinct graph mode in this harness / n too small for a meaningful tail) rather than estimated.

The bench itself gained **recall@10** and a **run-to-run recall@5 spread** (it previously reported only the mean); `baseline.json` refreshed with both + a `machine` field.

### 2 — Reconcile the `onnx` feature with reality (issue #125)

**The task expected a broken feature to fence — but investigation found the opposite: it was already repaired.** `crates/mnemo-core/src/embedding/onnx.rs` was migrated to the pinned `ort 2.0.0-rc.11` / `ndarray 0.17` / `tokenizers 0.23` API; `cargo build`+`test -p mnemo-core --features onnx` **build and pass (90 tests)**. What was never done: removing the CI exclusion, adding a job, or updating the docs — so **CI and five doc locations still said "broken/#125-open"** while `CHANGELOG.md` already said it was migrated. That contradiction is exactly the "third state" (docs disagree with code) the ask exists to eliminate.

Fencing a *working* feature with `compile_error!` would have been actively wrong. Instead:
- Added a dedicated **`onnx feature` CI job** (`cargo build`+`test -p mnemo-core --features onnx`) so it can't silently rot again.
- Reconciled the stale locations: `ci.yml` note, `README.md`, the `onnx.rs` module doc, and the v0.3.0 checklist now say it builds + is CI-covered.
- Kept honest about what's **not** done: end-to-end ONNX inference (and the ONNX MiniLM recall number) needs a real model on disk, which the build+test job doesn't fetch — that's the one open item on #125.

## Test plan

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` ✓
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --workspace --exclude mnemo-python` (`-D warnings`) ✓
- `cargo build --workspace --exclude mnemo-python` ✓
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude mnemo-python` ✓
- `cargo build -p mnemo-core --features onnx` + `cargo test -p mnemo-core --features onnx` ✓ (the new CI job)
- benchmark reproduced live (numbers above are from that run)

No version bump: neither item changes any public API. `check_version_drift.sh` stays red by design (the tag-gated publish is blocked on rotating the expired `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`, an operator action — unrelated to this PR).

Closes #44. Advances #125 (build/test repaired + CI-covered; model-fetch job remains).

items.title: feat: configurable rerank cut + manual eval CI (tasks 2.2, 2.5)
items.body:
Task 2.2 (the open H2 question): make the post-fusion candidate cut configurable via RERANK_CANDIDATES (env var, default 30) instead of a bare [:30]. A sweep on the real lfm index (30/50/100/9999) gives identical numbers (Recall@5 0.912 / MRR 0.716 / nDCG@5 0.760) because the unique candidate pool per query is only ~16-23 — always under 30. So the cut does not hurt recall; the knob stays for future tuning.

Task 2.5: add .github/workflows/eval.yml, a manual (workflow_dispatch) eval gate. Qdrant service container + CPU torch, indexes the sample corpus, runs the eval, fails on any drop below the saved sample baseline, and uploads the report as an artifact. Kept separate from the ML-free ci.yml.

Version bump and CHANGELOG entry for **v3.0.1**, covering #444, #450, #457 and the signature-check guard.

**Merge this last** — after #461, #462, #463 and #464 — so the tagged commit contains the fixes the entry describes.

## Why PATCH

Fixes only, no feature work, no change to simulated output. #444 adds header declarations (additive — nothing can depend on an *undeclared* tag), and the rest touch `scripts/delta/` and `tools/`, which the v3.0.0 public-API declaration explicitly excludes.

## Bumped

`Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `CITATION.cff`, and the **two** README references that mean *current version* — the comparison-table row and the download line.

## Deliberately NOT bumped

README's other `v3.0.0` mentions are **historical statements, not version pointers**:

- "Upgrading from 2.0.0 → 3.0.0"
- "As of **v3.0.0**, eidolon follows Semantic Versioning"
- "v3.0.0 renamed the tokens eidolon emits"
- the `v3.0.0+` column heading in the token table

Untouched by design — it needs the published tarball's `sha256`, so it follows the tag in its own commit.

It leads with the **pattern** rather than the list: every defect was in something that *measures* eidolon rather than in the simulation, and each reported a plausible number instead of failing — which is precisely why they went unnoticed.

It records the concrete before/after for the two most consequential ones — `call -m` destroying two of three CCF clusters, and the arithmetically impossible `manta_BND FP=39` inside `manta_overall FP=20` — so the reasoning survives in the repo without needing to read four PRs.

Full workspace suite green (28 groups, 0 failures); `cargo fmt --all --check` clean; `eidolon --version` reports `3.0.1`.

items.title: Ship the [vista] extra: VoyageVistaBackend (dense-embedding recall)
items.body:
Ports the internal Willow thought-buckets pipeline (`mint_buckets.py` + `wave.py` + `voyage_embed.py`) into willow-substrate as the first concrete backend under the extras foundation shipped in PR #9.

Substitutes for the dependency-free `VistaBackend` via the `RelationalBackend` Protocol; produces the same `VistaResult` shape so context / foveation / CLI / hooks read the surround unchanged whichever backend produced it.

## Algorithm

1. Read active events from the store.
2. Embed via **Voyage-4** with a per-event .npz cache next to the store. A corpus that grew by ten events only pays for those ten; model name is stamped into the cache header so different embedding dimensions never silently collide.
3. Cluster the vectors via **HDBSCAN** in cosine space; each cluster becomes a Vista. Vistas leave `mu={}` because the semantic centroid lives in a dense space that VistaBackend's sparse-vector API does not carry; the score gates use `semantic_score` populated directly by dense cosine similarity.
4. Embed the query, cosine-rank events, feed matches + explicit seeds into a **damped multi-hop spreading activation** over the co-occurrence graph derived from cluster membership. Degree-normalised so a dense cluster does not swamp a smaller one (the anti-seizure governor from `thought-buckets/wave.py`).
5. Return `VistaResult` with `reference_beams` + `matches` + `evidence` + `trace`, same shape as the dependency-free backend.

## Tests (6 new, **53/53 total** on `[vista]`-installed env)

- Import guard raises with a message naming `pip install "willow-substrate[vista]"` when the extra is absent; imports cleanly when present.
- Cosine matrix, HDBSCAN small-corpus fallback, canonical event text.
- End-to-end query with a **mock embedder** (no real Voyage calls in tests): seeds two clusters (connectome vs pricing) in 8-dim space, queries along the connectome axis, verifies top evidence comes from the semantically-matching cluster and reference beams carry positive weights.
- Empty-corpus early return.

## Additive

- Base install and its 47-test suite untouched.
- The new backend is opt-in via the `[vista]` extra.
- A caller who does not install it never imports its module and sees no behaviour change.

## Docs

`docs/EXTRAS.md`: updated the `[vista]` entry with a minimal usage example. README unchanged (still points at `EXTRAS.md`).

## Follow-up (PR N+2)

**Recall benchmark harness.** Comparative eval of the zero-dep floor vs `[vista]` vs BM25 on the temporal-sample corpus. Closes ChatGPT audit finding #4 and produces the numbers Peter's 'benchmarks for recall' ask needs.
