items.title: feat(benchmarks): measure retrieval quality with a golden dataset
items.body:
Closes #34.

Search **speed** was measured; search **quality** was not. "Relevance improved" was an opinion. This adds the harness that turns it into a number a reviewer can check and a regression can trip over.

## Results

| Mode | recall@1 | recall@5 | recall@10 | MRR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `lexical` (BM25) | 0.3765 | 0.6468 | 0.6983 | **0.6405** |
| `semantic` | — | — | — | UNAVAILABLE |
| `hybrid` | — | — | — | UNAVAILABLE |
| `hybrid+rerank` | — | — | — | UNAVAILABLE |

The three model-backed modes report `UNAVAILABLE` **with a reason and no numbers at all**. Scoring them needs fastembed weights downloaded at runtime, which would make the benchmark neither offline nor deterministic. An absent measurement must never be mistaken for a zero — inventing numbers here would repeat the mistake #22 fixed.

**This means the README's claim that hybrid + reranking improves accuracy is still untested.** The README now says so explicitly rather than implying it was verified.

## What the numbers say

| Intent | MRR | recall@1 | recall@10 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `exact-name` | 0.9333 | 0.7611 | 0.9333 |
| `behavioural` | 0.5893 | 0.3095 | 0.6905 |
| `conceptual` | 0.5667 | 0.1118 | 0.4614 |
| `paraphrase` | 0.3958 | 0.1944 | 0.6111 |

BM25 is near-perfect when the query names the symbol and less than half as good when it does not. That gap is the measurable case for the semantic leg — when weights are available offline, this table is where the improvement has to appear, and if it does not, the claim does not survive.

**A real defect the benchmark surfaced:** `q02` (`"UserService get_user"`) returns *nothing* relevant in the top 10, while `q31` (`"getUser"`) ranks a correct answer first. Naming the class repeats the token `user`, lifting bare `user` variables above the getter actually asked for — so qualifying a query with its class currently makes retrieval **worse**. Both queries are kept as a pair so the regression stays visible.

## Design decisions

- **Labels are `(file, qualified_name)` pairs, not symbol UIDs.** `CodeSymbol.uid` is a fresh UUID on every parse and cannot identify an answer across runs. A test asserts every label resolves to a real corpus symbol, so a renamed fixture fails loudly instead of quietly reporting a recall regression.
- **Tokenization is case-insensitive and splits identifiers**, so `format_name`, `formatName` and `GetUser` are the same token sequence. Labels reflect this and list every language variant — labelling only one would score the engine down for behaving correctly.
- **The dataset is data, not code.** Changing a judgement is a reviewable diff, so a metric movement traces to either a code change or a label change, never an invisible one. Every one of the 51 queries carries a written `rationale`.
- **Determinism is verified, not asserted.** Two runs over an unchanged tree produce byte-identical stdout and JSON; confirmed by diffing consecutive runs and guarded by tests. The only non-reproducible fields (`timestamp`, `commit_sha`) live in the baseline's provenance header and never touch a score.

## Contents

- `golden/queries.json` — 51 hand-labelled queries: exact-name (15), behavioural (14), paraphrase (12), conceptual (10)
- `src/eval/` — corpus loading, recall@k and MRR as pure functions, and the evaluator
- `retrieval-eval` binary — prints the table, writes a JSON report, re-records the baseline behind `--update-baseline`
- `corpus-inventory` binary — lists every retrievable symbol with the reference a label must use
- `benchmarks/METHODOLOGY.md` — labelling rules, metric definitions, and limitations stated plainly

## CI

The job is parked in `benchmarks/retrieval-quality-ci.yml`, **not** in `.github/workflows/`.

⚠️ **As merged, the retrieval-quality job does not run.** Tracked in #77.

This is not an oversight and it cannot be fixed on this branch: the App that opens these PRs has no `workflows` permission, so GitHub rejects the push at the server. Verified against the live remote:

```
 ! [remote rejected] HEAD -> probe-wf-perm-87371 (refusing to allow a GitHub App
   to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml` without `workflows` permission)
```

A maintainer enables it with one command — the parked file is a complete, valid workflow (`name`, `on`, one job), not a fragment to reassemble:

```bash
git mv benchmarks/retrieval-quality-ci.yml .github/workflows/retrieval-quality.yml
```

Report-only by design: a label fix and a genuine regression move the same number, and only a reviewer can tell them apart. The one thing that *does* fail the step is an unreadable report — a broken job rather than a judgement call.

Meanwhile the benchmark still runs by hand (`cargo run -p myceliums-benchmarks --bin retrieval-eval`), and the baseline provenance tests are ordinary `#[test]`s already covered by the existing `cargo test --workspace` job.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p myceliums-benchmarks --lib` — **42 passed, 0 failed**
- `cargo clippy -p myceliums-benchmarks --all-targets` — **zero warnings**
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- Two consecutive runs — byte-identical output

## Known limitations

96 symbols across five fixture projects, so absolute numbers characterise *this corpus* and are a regression tripwire, not a claim about real repositories. Single annotator, binary relevance (no graded judgements, so no nDCG), English-only queries, and three of four modes unmeasured.


## Follow-up commit: resolvable provenance

The baseline's `commit_sha` recorded a commit that ceased to exist once this branch was rebased onto `main`, so a reader could not check out the tree the numbers came from. Provenance that cannot be resolved is worse than none — it looks authoritative and is not.

Fixed by re-recording against a commit reachable from this branch, and by marking a dirty tree with a `-dirty` suffix so a baseline built from uncommitted code says so instead of implying a reproducibility it does not have.

Note that the sha names the tree the measurement *ran against*, which necessarily predates the commit carrying the file — a baseline cannot cite its own commit. The doc comment states this so the one-commit offset is not later mistaken for a bug. Metrics are byte-identical across the change; only the provenance header moved.

items.title: SIQ benchmark — Subconscious Injection Quality harness (#459)
items.body:
## What

Adds **SIQ (Subconscious Injection Quality)** — the flagship *native* benchmark from the benchmarking strategy (`docs/plans/benchmarking_strategy_2026-07.md` §2.1). It measures the one thing composite/query-blind retrieval does that no public benchmark scores: *without an explicit query cueing it, did the right memory get injected into context at the right turn?*

Plan: `docs/plans/siq_benchmark.md`. Closes #459.

## What it measures

Multi-turn agent traces where a later turn needs a memory established earlier, but the turn's own message never lexically restates it (coreference / implication / need-to-know). Retrieval runs through `ContextAssembler` in `composite` mode (query-blind). Metrics:

- **Injection Precision/Recall @ budget** — of memories injected under `max_items`/`max_tokens`, how many are ground-truth useful (evaluated at `should_recall` turns).
- **Anticipation lead time** — consecutive turns of proactive presence before a memory becomes explicitly relevant (a query retriever scores 0 by construction).
- **Budget efficiency** — useful-tokens / injected-tokens.

## Deterministic + competitor-fair

- **4 committed fixtures** (`coreference_relocation`, `implication_deadline`, `need_to_know_allergy`, `multi_recall_preferences`) — no runtime RNG, no wall-clock in ranking, bit-identical scores every run.
- **Cue-blindness lint** — `lint_trace` uses the real BM25 tokenizer to *prove* the recall-turn message shares no indexed token with the target memory (un-gameable ground truth).
- **`SiqAdapter` Protocol** — `NativeAdapter` (Popoto composite) + dependency-free `QueryOnlyStubAdapter` (query-driven baseline scoring ~0 recall / all-miss **by construction** — the harness's own validity proof). Real Mem0/Zep/Hindsight adapters are a tracked follow-up; **no competitor numbers fabricated**.

Baseline over the 4 fixtures: `native` recall **1.000** / 0-of-5 misses / mean lead **4.0** turns vs `query_stub` recall **0.000** / 5-of-5 misses / n/a.

## DB hygiene

CI-facing `tests/benchmarks/test_siq.py` runs under the pytest **db15** isolation plugin (never db0). The optional `run_siq.py` CLI reuses `run_external`'s bench-DB machinery (default 14, **db0 rejected**), pointed at only at `main()` time — point it away from any in-flight external run on db14 (`POPOTO_BENCH_DB=13`). Valkey-safe throughout (core Redis commands only).

## Tests

`pytest tests/benchmarks/test_siq.py` — 23 tests (lint rules, exact native scores, discriminant baseline, metric edge cases, composite-mode invariant, determinism, teardown residue, pinned-judge identity). `mkdocs build --strict` passes.

## Docs

`docs/benchmarks.md` gains a "Subconscious Injection Quality (SIQ) Harness" section (publishable); `tests/benchmarks/README.md` updated.

items.title: fix(search,bench): wire _use_ann flag; fix disk measurement in ingest benchmarks
items.body:
## What changed and why

### fix(search): wire up _use_ann flag - brute-force is now the default
Previously _use_ann was silently ignored (Rust underscore convention = unused). The engine always used HNSW when an index existed. Benchmarks show significant recall regression at lower dimensions (GloVe-200 b=4: 82.6% brute -> 36.1% ANN). This commit wires the flag through to the engine.

- search_with_filter_and_ann() and search_batch() now accept use_ann: bool
- ANN branch is gated: use_ann && has_index
- Python search() and query() pass _use_ann to the engine
- Default is False - brute-force is the safe, high-recall default; ANN is opt-in

### fix(bench): fix disk measurement inflation in ingest benchmarks
GROW_SLOTS pre-allocation inflated reported disk by ~18%. Fixed by calling db.close() before measuring file sizes. Also fixes UnicodeEncodeError on Windows cp1252 consoles.

### perf(storage): skip compaction on pure inserts (2-3x ingest throughput)
Compaction is skipped when no deletes are pending.

### bench(paper): update README tables and plots; auto-regenerate HTML dashboard

## Before/after recall

| Config | Brute recall | ANN recall (old, forced) |
|--------|-------------|--------------------------|
| GloVe-200 b=4 | 82.6% | 36.1% (-56%) |
| DBpedia-1536 b=4 | 95.5% | 79.9% |

With this fix, brute-force is used by default (matching the higher recall numbers).

items.title: Record real-embedding eval results + reranker rationale
items.body:
Records the first **real-embedding** eval run (`nomic-embed-text` via Ollama on an Apple M4) and the analysis it drives.

## Numbers (httpx==0.27.2)
| retriever | recall@10 | mrr | semantic | exact | cross |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| vector+nomic | **0.81** | **0.52** | 0.71 | **1.00** | 0.67 |
| hybrid+rrf | 0.81 | 0.46 | 0.71 | 0.75 | **1.00** |
| graph (PPR) | 0.762 | 0.31 | 0.57 | 0.50 | 1.00 |
| lexical | 0.762 | 0.34 | 0.57 | 0.75 | 1.00 |

## Findings
- **The embedder was the bottleneck.** vs the offline `hash` floor, the vector leg jumped: recall@10 0.67→**0.81**, MRR 0.31→**0.52**, SEMANTIC 0.43→**0.71**, EXACT 0.75→**1.0**.
- **With a strong embedder, equal-weight RRF underperforms the best single leg on ordering:** hybrid MRR (0.46) < vector MRR (0.52), because RRF dilutes the dominant vector signal with the weaker lexical/graph legs. Hybrid still ties on recall@10 and wins CROSS (1.0 vs 0.67).
- **This is the eval-doc's stated trigger for the reranker** ("add it only once RRF plateaus") — re-scoring the fused top-K should restore ordering without losing fusion's recall/CROSS coverage. Next M2 task.
- Caveat noted in the writeup: 21 questions is small (a 0.06 MRR gap ≈ one question).

Adds `eval/results-ollama.csv`; updates `eval/README.md` and the top-level README. Docs-only — no code change, tests unaffected.

## Summary
Second of four "P0 hardening" sub-projects before v1.0.0. Fixes a real data-leakage bug flagged by an external audit: Case 2 Lesson 6 ("Threshold Selection and Metric Choice") previously chose its classification decision threshold by comparing precision/recall/F1 for 0.5/0.3/0.2 **directly on the test set** — reusing the test set for a tuning decision.

- Adds `split_for_validation(train_df) -> (fit_df, val_df)`, carved from `train_df` using the same convention as the existing split.
- The three-threshold comparison now happens on `val_df` (model fit on `fit_df`), not `test_df`.

- Investigation before writing any code found the actual blast radius was much smaller than the audit implied: Lessons 5, 7, 8 needed **zero code changes**. Lesson 7's risk tiers use fixed, unrelated probability cutoffs; Lesson 8's `final_scorecard` already fit its model on the full `train_df`, so its existing numbers were never wrong — only the *reasoning* that arrived at threshold 0.2 was leaky. Verified: the fixed Lesson 6's final reveal reproduces Lesson 8's existing numbers exactly (precision 0.24444444444444444, recall 0.55, f1 0.3384615384615385).

items.title: fix(bench): seeding parity, canonical vector scoring, enforced allowlist (#162, #163, #164)
items.body:
Closes #162. Closes #163. Closes #164.

## 🔴 #162 — our own benchmark was handicapping us against ourselves

`--compare-rag` seeded Shonkor's capsule from **vector search alone**. Every shipped path — `search_hybrid`, `generate_capsule`, `/api/search/hybrid`, `/api/capsule` — seeds from **`HybridRetrieval`**, which has materially better intent recall (0,788 vs 0,697, per the numbers already in the README).

So the head-to-head was measuring **a configuration the product does not ship**, and losing with it.

### With seeding parity

| At a matched token budget | Coverage |
|---|--:|
| chunked-RAG (no graph) | 87,9 % |
| Shonkor — *vector-only seeds* | 84,8 % — **loses by 3,1 pp** |
| **Shonkor — as shipped (hybrid seeds)** | **93,9 % — wins by 6,1 pp** |

The previous PR published a **−3,1 pp loss** as a finding. It was an artefact of the harness.

### The vector-only arm stays

It isolates the graph's contribution (both sides from identical retrieval), and — more to the point — **deleting the unflattering row the moment a flattering one appears is exactly what these benchmarks exist to prevent**. `RagHeadToHead_StillPublishesTheArmWeLose` fails if anyone removes it from the README, and also fails if it ever *stops* losing without the prose being updated.

### The diagnosis is measured, not argued

Seed survival through the capsule budget is **100 %**, and in **5 of 33** vector-only misses the target was **never a seed at all**. The budget was not dropping the answer — retrieval never found it. That is precisely what #162 predicted, and it's now instrumented (`seedMissedTarget` in the metrics).

### ⚠️ The limitation I am not banking quietly

The baseline is **vector-only** and our winning row is **hybrid**. That's the conventional "naive RAG" setup, but a fair critic would say: give the chunks a keyword arm too. **They'd be right.** It's stated in the README *and* the sales deck, and filed as a follow-up. Until it's measured, the honest claim is *"the graph capsule beats naive chunked RAG"* — **not** *"vector retrieval is beaten."*

---

## #163 — score vectors the way the product does

`RagBaselineBenchmark.Cosine` was a hand-rolled loop accumulating in `double`, while storage scores L2-normalized embeddings with a **SIMD `float` dot product** (#127). Two summation semantics for one similarity — the exact inconsistency #127 removed from the product — living in the component whose entire job is producing trustworthy numbers. The baseline was being *ranked by arithmetic the product does not use*.

Now: `VectorMath.NormalizeL2` + `TensorPrimitives.Dot`.

**Verified, not assumed:** baseline coverage is **unchanged at 87,9 %**. Ranking is scale-invariant, so this is a consistency fix rather than a result change — which is what I predicted, and I checked rather than asserting it.

---

## #164 — the allowlist is no longer an honour system

`docs/symbol-allowlist.txt` is the escape hatch for the #159 guard. Its header said *"NEVER add a name here to silence a stale doc."* **A comment is not an enforcement mechanism.** Appending one line was the cheapest way to turn a red build green — leaving the doc stale **and** the guard reporting success, which is strictly worse than the original bug.

Three rules, now **enforced by the build**:

1. Every entry sits under a known `[category]` (`external-types`, `placeholders`, `config-values`, `deliberately-removed`).
2. Every entry carries a substantive `# reason`.
3. A `[deliberately-removed]` entry is only legitimate **while the docs still say the type was removed**. Delete that prose and the build fails — so `PluginLoader` cannot silently decay from "documented as gone" into "a dead symbol we agreed to stop noticing".

**Verified by mutation**, because a guard that cannot fail is not a guard:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Append a bare name to the allowlist | ❌ fails — no reason, no valid category |
| Delete the "**has been removed**" sentence about `PluginLoader` | ❌ fails — *"no doc still states that it was removed"* |
| Restore both | ✅ passes |

---

**379/379 tests green** (was 377).

## Better alternatives (separate from the shipped change)

- **Give the chunked-RAG baseline a keyword arm.** This is the honest counterpart to #162 and the reason I would not let the +6,1 pp stand unqualified. Right now we compare *Shonkor-hybrid* against *RAG-vector-only*. A BM25-over-chunks arm fused into the baseline would tell us whether the graph is winning, or merely hybrid retrieval is. Until then the win is real but narrower than it looks. → filing.
- **The vector-only arm is now dead weight in the shipped product's story.** It exists to isolate the graph's contribution, and it costs a second full capsule synthesis per query (the run does both). If the isolation is only ever interesting to us, it belongs behind a flag rather than in every `--compare-rag` run. Left in deliberately for now — it is the row that keeps us honest — but it doubles the benchmark's capsule work. → filing.

items.title: feat(eval): falsify the thesis. semantic-dedup harness, curated dataset, honest results
items.body:
## goal

prove or disprove the product thesis with measurement, not anecdote.

the claim 'semantic intent dedup catches real llm retries reliably and safely' was demonstrated on hand-crafted near-duplicates but never measured against precision and recall. operators had no way to tune semantic_threshold except by guessing. this pr ships the harness, the dataset, the numbers, and the policy defaults that the numbers point at.

## what is in the pr

- new internal/eval package mirrors the proxy's normalize+fingerprint+intent-string code so the eval cannot drift from production behavior. Runner scores every pair, BuildPairs walks every same-tool combination, Evaluate sweeps thresholds across [0.50, 0.99] in 0.01 steps, BestThreshold picks highest f1 per tool with a tie-break toward conservative thresholds.
- new cmd/potent-eval cli. accepts a jsonl dataset and a policy yaml, emits a human table or json document.
- new docs/eval/dataset.jsonl. 51 records, 5 tools (send_email, charge_card, create_task, delete_user, search_web), 4-8 intents per tool, each with whitespace, reorder, synonym, and paraphrase variants, plus adversarial negatives that share template words with positives but differ on a load-bearing field (different recipient, different amount, opposite verb, different priority, different topic).
- new docs/eval/methodology.md describes how the dataset was built and what it does not test.
- new docs/eval/results.md ships the honest numbers and a per-tool recommendation.
- ci workflow gains a semantic-eval job that runs the harness on every push and uploads the json artifact for regression tracking.
- configs/policy.yaml semantic_threshold values updated from guessed defaults to calibrated values, with comments pointing at the methodology.
- readme replaces 'semantic catches llm retries' with a section that links to the results and notes the precision/recall tradeoff.

## the headline numbers

| tool | best threshold | precision | recall | fpr | f1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| send_email | 0.73 | 0.559 | 1.000 | 0.128 | 0.717 |
| charge_card | 0.91 | 0.375 | 0.750 | 0.156 | 0.500 |
| create_task | 0.85 | 0.462 | 0.857 | 0.241 | 0.600 |
| delete_user | 0.99 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 |
| search_web | 0.81 | 0.625 | 0.455 | 0.055 | 0.526 |

at threshold 0.9 (the readme's prior default) send_email recall drops to 0.263. the embedder misses 74% of paraphrases an llm would realistically produce. for charge_card the semantic tier produces 5 false positives at any reasonable threshold. for short queries (search_web) recall caps at 0.455 below a 10% fpr.

## honest verdict

the mechanism works as designed. whitespace/casing/reorder retries are caught reliably. paraphrases are caught partially. for structured/numeric tools the semantic tier is at best neutral and at worst harmful. the readme's pre-1.0 admission about the hashing-tfidf limits is validated by the data. onnx swap is the next step and this eval will be rerun when it ships.

## test plan

- [x] go test -race -cover ./...  all packages >= 80%; eval at 87.9%
- [x] go vet / staticcheck / gosec clean
- [x] make eval reproduces the numbers in docs/eval/results.md
- [x] make eval-json emits valid json
- [x] curated dataset parses without errors
- [x] new TestLoadDataset_DatasetFile_IsValid asserts the dataset has at least 30 records and every record has tool+intent_id+args
- [x] ci semantic-eval job runs the harness on push
- [ ] after merge: cut v0.1.9 to publish the eval and the new policy defaults

items.title: feat: cert back-test over decided petitions (selection, lift, calibration, replay)
items.body:
Sets up the cert back-test issue #182 asks for — the measurement harness, ready to run. (Not `Closes #182`: the issue's acceptance also includes actually running it over real petitions and capturing findings, which needs the corpus + a token budget decision — see "Running it" below.)

## What's here

- **`select_cert_backtest_set`** — resolved SCOTUS **modern discretionary-cert** petitions (`corpus.is_modern_cert`, the Term-prefixed post-1925 form) with a machine-readable grant/deny label and consistent dates, most recently decided first so a small `--limit` reads on recent cert practice. This folds in the #309 selection caveat from the issue's status update: mandatory-jurisdiction and application/original regimes are excluded up front, so the label space stays comparable.
- **`run_cert_backtest`** — per predictor: accuracy, granted-accuracy, Brier, **lift over the always-deny floor** (the honest signal under the denial skew, and the rank key), and a decile **calibration** view of P(granted) vs the observed grant rate. The report carries the floor's accuracy (`always_denied_accuracy`) and is labeled `stratum: "retrospective"` — the cert back-test adopts the leaderboard's pre-registration stratification rather than inventing its own, per #439's design.
- **`replay_predictors`** — the agentic half through the same engine-runner seam `run-predict` uses: for each petition it provisions a **redacted snapshot** (`redact_snapshot` strips every field that exists only because the matter was decided — disposition, termination/decision/cert/argument dates, clusters, citations, opinion text, and docket entries wholesale, since the disposing order lives there) plus the event definition **as it looked while open**, into a scratch tree — never `data/`. One cell per enabled predictor per petition; `stub`/`replay` engines run it offline (tested end-to-end), a real engine spends tokens.
- **`fedcourts cert-backtest`** CLI → `metrics/cert-backtest.json` (`--out`): offline reference baselines (always-deny floor, prior-vote) by default; `--engine claude-code|codex|gemini` adds the agentic replay; `--limit` (default 25) caps spend.
- New `CertBacktest`/`CertBacktestEntry`/`CalibrationBin` schemas, exported; docs rows in `docs/cli.md` and `metrics/README.md`.

## What redaction can and cannot do

Redaction keeps the *file inputs* outcome-free, mirroring `BacktestFeatures`' withholding. What it cannot remove is a model's parametric memory of a decided case — which is exactly why the report is labeled retrospective and its numbers read as recall + calibration + label-mapping fit, not foresight. That framing is in the schema description and module docstring.

## Running it (the follow-up this PR tees up)

1. **Dry run, zero tokens:** `fedcourts cert-backtest --limit 25` where the corpus is pulled — offline baselines only, confirms the selection and the always-deny floor over real petitions.
2. **Agentic run:** `fedcourts cert-backtest --limit 10 --engine claude-code` (~one predict cell per predictor per petition, ≈$0.50/cell at measured rates — keep N small). Then the issue's remaining acceptance: read a sample of the replayed `reasoning.md` for cert-signal soundness, note where `predict.md` strains on cert, and open the prompt-tuning follow-up.

## Verification

- 733 tests pass (10 new: selection filters + recency order + limit, redaction, lift math, calibration bins incl. the closed top bin, lift-then-Brier ranking, empty set, stub-engine replay end-to-end over the fixture corpus — asserting the provisioned snapshot is redacted, the event reads unresolved, and nothing lands outside the scratch tree — and the CLI both with replay and against an absent corpus).
- `ruff`, `mypy --strict`, `fedcourts validate data` green; `schemas/` regenerated (19 schemas, +`cert_backtest`).

items.title: refactor(relationships,reducer): centralize correlation confidence into documented registries
items.body:
Closes #3490

## What

Correlation confidence values were hand-tuned magic constants scattered as inline `float64` literals across ~15 `relationships` extractor files and the `reducer` candidate loader, with no central provenance, no documented rationale per value, and no test guarding their relative ordering. The Bayesian corroboration math in `resolver.go` was principled; its inputs were not auditable or calibratable.

This centralizes both confidence taxonomies into single, documented, overridable registries and pins the confidence semantics with invariant tests:

- **`go/internal/relationships/confidence.go`** — `DefaultConfidenceRegistry`, keyed by `EvidenceKind`, each entry carrying a value, a `ConfidenceTier`, and a rationale. Named family accessors cover the runtime-service and schema-driven Terraform extractors whose `EvidenceKind` strings are computed at runtime.
- **`go/internal/reducer/workload_signal_confidence.go`** — `DefaultWorkloadSignalConfidence`, keyed by `WorkloadSignalKind`, each entry carrying a value, a `WorkloadSignalTier`, and a rationale.

Both registries are immutable after construction and expose `WithOverrides(...)` for calibration without editing source or mutating the shared default. All extractors and the candidate loader now read their priors from the registries instead of inline literals.

## Why this is safe (no correlation-truth change)

Every emitted confidence value is **byte-identical** to the prior inline literal (registries are built once at package init and read by O(1) map lookup; provenance kind strings are unchanged). This is a pure structural refactor — no evidence, candidate, resolved-relationship, or workload-admission behavior changes.

## Invariants pinned (written failing-first, TDD)

- every `EvidenceKind` / `WorkloadSignalKind` has a documented registry entry (a new kind without one fails the build)
- every value is within `[0,1]`
- tier floors are strictly monotonic; each registered value respects its declared tier floor
- **ordering / monotonicity**: direct-binding > strong-reference > reference > weak-reference; and on the reducer side, runtime signals strictly outrank CI/controller provenance
- the calibration override hook validates bounds and never mutates the default
- the schema-driven resource-name fallback weight stays below `DefaultConfidenceThreshold`

## Follow-up

Full statistical calibration (golden-set precision/recall per evidence kind to re-derive the absolute numbers, and justify the 0.75 threshold from the curve) remains future work. These registries are the structural prerequisite: the numbers now live in one auditable, overridable place instead of scattered literals.

## Evidence

- `cd go && go test ./internal/relationships ./internal/reducer -count=1` → 2406 pass (incl. unchanged `resolver_confidence_test.go`, `evidence_test.go`, `candidate_loader_test.go`)
- `cd go && go test ./internal/query ./internal/mcp ./cmd/reducer ./cmd/ingester -count=1` → 4033 pass
- new focused tests: `go test ./... -run 'Confidence|WorkloadSignal'` → all pass
- `golangci-lint run ./internal/relationships/... ./internal/reducer/...` → 0 issues
- `scripts/verify-package-docs.sh`, `scripts/verify-performance-evidence.sh` → pass
- `git diff --check` → clean
- docs updated: `relationships` README + AGENTS, `reducer` README (registry model, tier tables, No-Regression / No-Observability-Change markers)

items.title: Enhancements to VDB benchmark script
items.body:
Merging in enhancements from Alessandro Goncalves:
Keeping the original benchmark script and recall functionality in the repository. Thus, README is updated to reflect all the changes and steps for running the complete workflow.

An `enhanced_bench`  to calculate collection performance. One point that was missing is the ability to get recall numbers that are local to the host / environment. To do that you need to get a Ground Truth , a FLAT INDEX with the same Vector / Dimension / Seed as the collections you want to evaluate.

1. Running the benchmark it will look for the ground truth. I changed to load_vdb.py to create the GT collection if not available. This GT will be the same for all indexes with the same settings.
2. It will set a recall target.
3. It will sweep the collection for the best performance meeting the recall target. QPSxRecall 
4. Has a cold and warm cache search
5. It will show the max_throughput , regardless of the recall. (Highest QPS)
6. DiskANN and AISAQ --> Search list has to be higher for the search part to get the recall. I was testing and only got 15% recall, which is very poor. The reason was the search_list was too small , about 200. Bumped for 3000 and got better recall results.

items.title: fix: capstone methodological correctness (feature-scoped imputation, stratified split, cluster stability, saved scaler)
items.body:
## Summary

PR 4 of the "release polish" arc (third external audit, 2026-07-14). Fixes four real methodological gaps in Capstone Lessons 4-6, plus reverses one of my own earlier calls on the second audit.

- **`impute_missing` scoped to features (audit #3)**: was `impute_missing(train_df, test_df)`, iterating *every* column of `train_df` — a latent risk (nothing broken today, since no target column has missing values, but an unsafe pattern). Now `impute_missing(train_df, test_df, feature_columns)`, touches only the columns you tell it to.
- **Stratified split for classification (audit #3)**: `split_dataset` gained an optional `stratify_column` param; the `lendwell_loan_default` path (~15.8% positive class) now passes `stratify_column="defaulted"`. Verified real impact: model precision `0.5→0.25`, f1 `0.133→0.118` (recall coincidentally unchanged).
- **Clustering evaluation, reframed — revised mid-design**: the original ask (audit #2 and #3 both) was "clustering isn't evaluated on held-out data like regression/classification." I initially discussed a train/test split fix, then checked this repo's own Case 3 (the dedicated clustering case) and found it **never** splits for clustering — it evaluates quality via full-dataset silhouette and stability via resampling + ARI. A train/test split would have taught a second, inconsistent methodology. Instead: `evaluate_clustering`'s body is untouched (full-dataset silhouette is correct, matches Case 3), and a new `cluster_stability` function — ported from Case 3 Lesson 7's `subsample_stability` — is added to Lesson 5, checking how much cluster assignments move under repeated 80% resampling (ARI). README/notebook wording updated to stop implying clustering is held-out-evaluated.
- **`scale_features` returns its fitted scaler (audit #3)**: was `-> pd.DataFrame`, discarding the fitted `StandardScaler`. This repo's own design brief explicitly scopes "saving a pipeline" as acceptable basic deployment content (distinct from out-of-scope "full MLOps"). Now returns `(scaled_df, scaler)`.

## Verified numbers

- Regression: **zero impact** — baseline `41.521249999999995`, model MAE `10.600387466214906`, all Lesson 4/5/6 assertions unchanged.
- Classification: baseline unchanged (`0`/`0.0`/`0.0`/`0.0`); **model changed** — precision `0.5→0.25`, f1 `0.13333333333333333→0.11764705882352941`, recall unchanged (`0.07692307692307693`, coincidence).
- Clustering: **zero impact** on existing numbers (silhouette `0.22231830884063178`, sizes `[108,92,50]`, shares `0.432/0.368/0.2` all unchanged).
- New `cluster_stability` (k=3, fraction=0.8, seeds 0-4): ARI `1.0, 0.298486552621068, 0.3099899620816333, 0.9000942897023166, 0.949562686665437` — a realistic, pedagogically useful spread, not a number to "fix."

## Test plan

- [x] `LESSON_MODULE=solution uv run pytest -q` — Lesson 4: 9 passed, Lesson 5: 4 passed, Lesson 6: 4 passed; Lessons 1-3 unaffected (8/13/12).
- [x] `task.py` scaffolding fails cleanly with `NotImplementedError` in all three lessons.
- [x] All three notebooks executed end-to-end with `solution.py` swapped in, for **all three** `DATASET_NAME` branches each (not just the committed default) — 9 notebook executions total, all clean.
- [x] `uv run ruff check .` clean (caught and fixed two real issues during implementation: an F821 from a quoted `StandardScaler` forward-reference, fixed via `TYPE_CHECKING` guard; a docstring line-length violation).
- [x] `uv run python tools/check_bilingual_pairs.py` — 42/42 paired.
- [x] Per-task review (3 subagent passes, one per lesson) + final whole-branch review (opus) — zero unresolved findings. Caught and fixed one notebook JSON formatting regression (missing trailing newline) via `nbformat` normalization.

## Out of scope

Cluster profiles in raw (non-z-score) units (PR 5 — reverses my own earlier "leave as-is" call on the second audit, see conversation), Pipeline/ColumnTransformer content, calibration/uncertainty content, responsible-AI module, task.py scaffolding reduction, instructor guide — all separate PRs later in the same release-polish arc. The `v1.0.0` tag is not part of this PR.

items.title: fix: normalize indexed repo paths in eval runner, calibrate baseline
items.body:
## What

The retrieval-quality eval harness (#312) scored `recall 0` across every query on its first calibration run. Root cause was a path-format mismatch, not a bad ranker:

- **Index stores:** `repos/<repo_id>/<path>` (e.g. `repos/78aa181e-.../backend/middleware/auth.py`)
- **Ground-truth labels:** repo-root-relative (`backend/middleware/auth.py`)

The two never string-matched, so `ranx` computed 0 recall even though `search_v2` was returning the right files at rank 1.

## Fix

Strip the exact `repos/<repo_id>/` storage prefix in the runner before matching (`_to_repo_relative`). Exact match on `repo_id` so a path that merely starts with `repos/` is never over-trimmed. `queries.json` stays repo-root-relative and portable across repo_ids (honors the `OCI_EVAL_REPO_ID` override design).

## Calibration result

Ran against the OCI repo index over the 10-query ground-truth set:

| Tier | recall@10 | MRR |
|---|---|---|
| Free (core ranker) | 0.80 | 0.80 |
| Pro (Cohere rerank) | 0.85 | 0.658 |

`baseline.json` now has the free-tier numbers with `calibrated: true`, so `pytest evals/ -v` asserts (`recall@10 >= 0.75`) instead of skipping. Verified passing locally.

## Notes

- Free-tier (deterministic, no Cohere) is the CI regression baseline, per the harness README.
- Reranking is **not strictly better** on this set: +0.05 recall@10 but MRR drops 0.80 -> 0.658 (pulls one extra expected file into top-10 while demoting rank-1 hits). Worth a follow-up look at the pro-tier default.
- Known ranker misses: q06 (durable repo-state) and q10 (path-filtering) — tracked separately, not addressed here.

## Test plan

- [x] `python -m evals` returns real numbers (free + pro tiers)
- [x] `pytest evals/ -v` passes against the calibrated baseline

items.title: Flip-TTA at the deployment operating points: measured, and not worth 2× GPU (#78)
items.body:
Closes #78.

## What this measures

The evaluated configuration (`stage_two/evaluate.py`, horizontal-flip TTA) and the deployed detector (single-pass) have differed by an unmeasured delta since sidewalk-auto-labeler#3. This rides #54's low-floor extraction exactly as the issue prescribed: a second `extract --tta` arm (mirrored heatmap un-flipped and maxed with the original — numerically identical to `evaluate.py`'s composition, with tests asserting the clip-order equivalence), swept post-hoc on identical GT alongside the single-pass arm. `manual_gold` needed no GPU pass: its committed detections *are* a TTA export at the 0.05 floor, so the records supplied that arm.

## What flip-TTA actually is

For anyone reading this cold: it is the obvious thing. Run the panorama through the model; mirror the panorama and run it again; un-mirror that second heatmap back into pano orientation; combine the two. Nothing is retrained — it is purely an inference-time trick that costs a second forward pass.

**The combine rule is where the entire result comes from.** `stage_two/evaluate.py:191` composes with elementwise `np.maximum`, not an average.

Two reasons this was worth running even though the outcome is negative:

1. **The accounting reason, which was the real driver.** `--tta` defaults to `True` in `evaluate.py`, commented "as in the paper" — so every committed gold-set number is a TTA number, while the deployed labeler is single-pass. Sizing that gap was mandatory regardless of whether TTA turned out to be worth deploying.
2. **The ensembling hope.** Two views, partly uncorrelated errors, and RampNet is recall-first (a false negative is a permanently missed ramp; a false positive is cheap to reject downstream). A cheap recall lever deserved a measurement.

## The answer

**Pooled US (609 panos): TTA at the deployed 0.55 buys +2.4 recall points for −1.1 precision — but after the #54 threshold drop to 0.30, the marginal value collapses to +0.9 R / −2.4 P, with F1 *down* on four of the five US splits.** TTA is a mild threshold-lowering in disguise (its recall curve is the single-pass curve shifted left — see the committed figure), so the free lever absorbs almost everything the 2×-GPU lever would buy. AP spans −0.012 (annapolis) to +0.014 (morgantown), +0.004 pooled.

| lever (from single@0.55, pooled US) | ΔR | ΔP | ΔF1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| threshold drop alone (0.55→0.30) | **+0.074** | −0.068 | +0.016 |
| TTA alone (at 0.55) | +0.024 | −0.011 | +0.011 |
| both | +0.083 | −0.092 | +0.009 |
| **TTA after the drop (at 0.30)** | **+0.009** | **−0.024** | **−0.007** |

`manual_gold` (in-domain control) is the one exception — marginal +1.9 R / −1.5 P, AP 0.904 → 0.917 — so the paper's TTA evaluation was a reasonable in-domain choice; it just doesn't transfer to deployment imagery. And the configuration mismatch is now quantified and closed: TTA-evaluated numbers read **+2.4 recall points above** what single-pass deployment delivers at 0.55.

**Negative result, recorded deliberately: no production TTA knob gets filed in sidewalk-auto-labeler.** The #78 plan filed it only if TTA won at the chosen operating point; it loses there. The 0.30 single-pass recommendation from #54 is unchanged.

## Why the mechanism produces exactly this result

Both halves of the finding fall out of two properties of the setup, neither of them specific to this benchmark. This is now written into `docs/operating_point.md` so the reasoning survives with the numbers.

**Max-combine can only *add* detections.** Because the two passes combine pixelwise by max, the TTA heatmap is **pointwise ≥** the single-pass heatmap everywhere. At a fixed threshold, TTA can promote a detection but can never suppress one. That is the mechanical reason it behaves as a threshold change rather than merely correlating with one: the two levers are the same *kind* of operation — both admit weaker evidence, trading precision for recall. Hence "threshold-lowering in disguise" is a description of the operator, not an analogy.

(An *averaging* TTA would be a different animal: a variance reducer, able to remove false positives as well as add true ones. That is not what the paper used and not what these numbers measure. It remains untested.)

**The model was already trained to be flip-invariant.** `stage_two/train.py:202-207` applies random horizontal flip at p = 0.5, correctly relabelling `x → 1 − x`; the crop models do the same (`stage_one/crop_model/*/train.py:71`). Test-time flipping can therefore only exploit whatever asymmetry the *training-time* flip failed to remove. **A small gain is the expected outcome, not an anomaly** — training aug and test aug are the same transform pointed at the same invariance, and the better the former worked, the less the latter can find.

Read the other way, this makes the marginal TTA gain a measurement: it says how much the two views still disagree in a way that matters at the operating point. At ≤1.3 recall points per US split, the answer is "barely" — the training augmentation did its job.

### What this does *not* say — follow-up filed as #82

That second point also bounds the scope of the negative result. The horizontal flip is the **only** augmentation in the training recipe: the input transform is `Resize(2048×4096) → ToTensor → Normalize` (`train.py:224-229`), with no photometric, scale, or other geometric variation, on either the pano model or the crop models.

So #78 establishes that the one invariance that *was* trained for is saturated. It says nothing about the ones that were never trained for — and the benchmark's live failure mode is cross-city transfer (GT-measured recall at 0.55 spans richmond 0.895 down to clovis 0.650). #82 takes that up: **yaw-roll and photometric jitter**, which are the two augmentations that are simultaneously legal on an equirectangular projection and untried. Worth noting for anyone reaching for the standard list — in-plane rotation and perspective warp are *not* legal here (the top and bottom image rows are the poles; an image-plane rotation mixes pole with horizon and destroys the projection), whereas horizontal roll is exactly a camera yaw, wraps seamlessly, and is exactly label-preserving.

## What's in the PR

- `operating_point_curve.py extract --tta` + arm guard (TTA and single-pass caches cannot share a directory — extract's resume-skip would otherwise silently score one arm as the other), arm-aware parity gate, `low_floor_sweep.py tta` with the four-lever decomposition, `plot_tta.py` + committed figure, the `docs/operating_point.md` section (including the caveat direction: the #55 GT bias overstates TTA's marginal precision cost if anything, and the exact marginal recall gain is too small to price 2× GPU against), and the reproduce/README updates.
- The mechanism subsection above, and a `#82` entry in "What would change this" — better transfer would move the 0.30 threshold itself, since part of what 0.30 is compensating for is out-of-domain under-confidence.
- 241 tests pass. Run log and interim results are in the #78 comments.

items.title: Rebuild the payee population as a power law, and the two artifacts it was hiding
items.body:
## Scope note first

This is larger than one session's work. PR #3 squash-merged on 2026-07-23 and **four commits have accumulated on this branch since without ever reaching `main`**, so `main` is currently missing `tests/test_ledger.py` entirely, has older copies of `test_campaigns.py` / `test_features.py`, and still documents metrics that were corrected days ago. Those earlier commits are included here because the newer work builds directly on them (the point-in-time pipeline, and `test_ledger.py` itself).

| commit | date | status before this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `d3d31ab` point-in-time skew fix | 07-24 | unmerged |
| `3409d4f` stale-number cleanup | 07-24 | unmerged |
| `3d22543` ring/herd fan-in + determinism fix | 07-25 | unmerged |
| `33c9ba7` payee population rebuilt as a power law | 07-27 | unmerged |

## Headline: out-of-time AUC moves 0.894 to 0.869, and the decrease is the result

The recipient/network feature family rested on a **flat payee id space**, which breaks it whichever direction it is flat in. Both flavours had shipped at some point:

**Narrow** (8,000 slots shared by ~1,450 customers). The birthday paradox alone made every payee look shared: median legitimate payee had 25 distinct senders against 21 for fraud-touched, so fan-in was collision noise carrying no behavioural information. Worse, the space saturated well before the train/test cutoff, so legitimate traffic could not pay a never-before-seen account **at all**: 0.0% of held-out legit rows hit an unseen payee, against 11.3% of fraud. "I have never seen this payee" was a **452x** fraud giveaway, and part of the previous recall was quietly being bought from it.

**Wide** (~10M slots, tried and reverted). Removed the collisions and every trace of shared structure with them. Nearly every payee had exactly one sender, the reputation table blew up to 207k mostly single-sighting entries, recipient history could only be memorised rather than generalised, and catch rate on genuinely new recipients fell to 0.2%.

Replaced with **one Zipf-weighted payee population**: the head is the shared merchants, the deep tail is private payees, and the continuum between them is what makes fan-in a graded signal instead of a flag. The exponent was swept against the realized distribution rather than guessed. At `s=1.15` the top payee was paid by 1,449 of 1,450 customers and the 90th-percentile *transaction* also saw a fan-in of 1,449, so "high fan-in" would have carved off the negative class wholesale. At `s=0.7` the distribution grades properly (median 2, p90 14, most popular payee 545 of 1,450, i.e. a supermarket rather than a universal utility) and puts 50% of legitimate transactions in the same 2-5 fan-in band a covered mule occupies.

### Camouflage reworked, not turned up

The flat space had been supplying some camouflage by accident, which is why a previous attempt to compensate by simply raising the mule-cover rate failed. The old mechanism drew a **fresh random sender for every cover payment**, so a mule with 14 payments had ~14 distinct senders and read as a small merchant; raising it to 30 made it read as a large one. Neither is what a recruited account looks like. Cover now draws a small sender set **once** and pays repeatedly from inside it (2-5 distinct senders, 2-10 payments each), which lands the mule in the personal-payee fan-in band that the power-law universe now genuinely populates on both sides.

### Measured, held out out-of-time

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| novelty asymmetry (fraud vs legit on an unseen payee) | 452x | **1.33x** |
| legit rows paying someone new | 0.0% | 5.1% |
| fan-in per payee | median 25 (noise) | median 2, p90 4, p99 11, max 515 |
| fraud-touched payees inside the clean IQR | 29.1% | 40.7% |
| reputation density (legit / fraud seeing a known payee) | 100% / 89% | 95% / 93% |
| model AUC | 0.894 | 0.869 |

`README.md` has been updated to say plainly that the number went down and why, rather than quoting the higher one.

## A judgment call worth reviewing

`MULE_TARGET_TRAFFIC`'s lower bound is set from the leak audit, not from taste. At a floor of 2 a campaign's handful of fraud rows landed on a tiny denominator and `recipient_global_fraud_rate` reached a solo AUC of **0.9290**, past this repo's own 0.90 "suspicious, go look at the generator" bar and close to the 0.9675 oracle the remap mechanism exists to prevent. Three settings were measured, and **the chosen one is not the one with the best headline numbers**:

| traffic band / cover | solo AUC | model AUC | recall @FPR 0.34% | recall on unseen-payee fraud |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (2, 80) / (1, 7) | 0.9290 over bar | 0.904 | 8.3% | 49.6% |
| **(5, 150) / (2, 10)** | **0.8948** | 0.869 | 9.1% | **57.5%** |
| (10, 250) / (3, 14) | 0.8730 | **0.911** | **11.2%** | **0.8%** |

The last row scores best and has a structural blind spot: cover the mules that heavily and known-payee fraud becomes the cheapest thing to catch, so the scorer spends every alert there and stops flagging brand-new accounts altogether. A system that never alerts on a payment to an account nobody has ever paid is not a better system, it is one with a hole in the place that matters most. The middle row is preferred on that basis rather than on AUC.

## Negative result: `recipient_fan_in` is still not shipped

It stays computed and tested but out of the trained feature list, now for a measured reason rather than a caveat. Its old solo AUC of 0.7056 **was** the novelty artifact; on the reworked population it is 0.52. Trained in anyway it makes the model worse (AUC 0.904 to 0.897) and drives recall on unseen-payee fraud to 0.0% at tight budgets, because `fan_in` is 0 for an unseen payee and ordinary legitimate traffic now hits unseen payees ~5% of the time, so the model learns to read a zero as reassuring and suppresses exactly the alerts that matter.

## Reproducibility bug found en route

Two call sites built a `set` of recipient ids and iterated it while drawing from `rng`. Set iteration order depends on the interpreter's per-process string hash seed, not just `random.Random`'s seed, so `--seed 20260720` was silently producing a different ledger on every run. Fixed with `dict.fromkeys`; verified byte-identical output across runs under different `PYTHONHASHSEED` values. Every before/after measured before this fix was noisier than it appeared.

## `leak_audit.py`: three real bugs in the safety tool itself

1. Reputation was **always** passed as `None`, so `recipient_global_fraud_rate` and `recipient_fan_in`, the model's most important feature family, were silently zero-filled in every audit ever run.
2. Fixing that surfaced a second bug: the combined check bucketed by entity while reputation used a temporal split, producing a false 0.9993 "leak" from the mismatch itself.
3. The default `--limit 300000` took a chronological prefix of a timestamp-sorted ledger, which starves the held-out side of a temporal split, and the guard returned the same shape as a clean result (`0.5` / `{}`) instead of erroring. It now defaults to no limit and raises loudly on a starved bucket.

## Verification

Final `leak_audit.py` on the shipped ledger: **zero findings**.

```
recipient_global_fraud_rate   0.8948   (under the 0.90 bar)
recipient_fan_in              0.5376
all features (linear)         0.9331   (under the 0.98 bar)
network family alone          0.6235   (was 0.6966)

No single feature and no single family separates the classes.
```

Tests: 53/54 pass. Four new payee-graph guards in `test_ledger.py`, each mutation-checked against the real historical defect it describes (both flat id spaces, and the old cover shape). The popularity guard needed strengthening after its first version passed under **both** defects: the discriminating statistic is the spread (p99/median is 8.5 power-law, 3.0 narrow, 1.0 wide), not the median, which is 1-2 in all three. The single failure (`test_point_in_time_refuses_out_of_order_rows`) needs the `pytest` package for `pytest.raises` and is a pre-existing environment gap unrelated to these changes.

## Method note now in the README

Recall at a fixed threshold is not comparable across models. A change that makes the scorer more conservative lowers recall and the false positive rate together and reads as a regression when the ranking actually improved. Every before/after here is quoted at a matched alert budget or matched FPR.
